papers.title: Sinkhole susceptibility and genesis at the southwestern slope of the Mount Sirino (Basilicata, Southern Italy): insights from field survey and machine learning modeling
papers.source: Rendiconti online della Società Geologica Italiana
papers.summary: The southwestern slope of the Mount Sirino (Basilicata, Southern Italy) is characterized by complex geological conditions favouring heterogeneous sinkhole phenomena. The most prominent geomorphological feature is Lake Sirino, formed on a large landslide deposit and frequently affected by piping-related sinkhole phenomena. This study uses an integrated approach combining geological and geomorphological surveys, remote sensing and machine learning modelling to investigate the genetic mechanisms of sinkhole formation at Lake Sirino and its surrounding areas (c. 100 km²). Fieldwork identified ten natural sinkholes, mainly associated with deep-seated piping processes in detrital deposits overlying low-permeability substrate. The Maximum Entropy (MaxEnt) algorithm was used to create a susceptibility map of natural sinkholes in the study area. This analysis identified lithology and fault density as the primary predisposing factors. The results highlight that sinkholes development in the Lake Sirino area is controlled by the interaction between high hydraulic gradients, fractured zones, and contrasting permeability layers.

papers.title: Landslide Susceptibility and Runout Modelling Along the Karakoram Highway Using PS-InSAR and Hybrid CNN-LSTM–XGBoost
papers.summary: The Karakoram Highway (KKH) traverses a tectonically active and climatically sensitive mountain corridor that is repeatedly affected by landslides. This study develops an integrated hybrid framework combining convolutional neural network–long short-term memory (CNN-LSTM) learning, extreme gradient boosting (XGBoost), persistent-scatterer interferometric synthetic aperture radar (PS-InSAR), runout modelling, climate projections, and multi-hazard risk assessment along a 320-km section of the KKH in northwestern Pakistan. Eighteen topographic, hydrological, geological, climatic, anthropogenic, and geodetic conditioning factors were used. The CNN-LSTM was pre-trained on the NASA Cooperative Open Online Landslide Repository and fine-tuned using an inventory of 612 landslides, while class imbalance was addressed using SMOTE and focal loss. The stacked hybrid model achieved an AUC of 0.974, accuracy of 0.928, and Cohen’s κ of 0.856, outperforming standalone CNN-LSTM (AUC = 0.951) and XGBoost (AUC = 0.938) models. SHAP and Grad-CAM analyses identified slope, PS-InSAR line-of-sight velocity, annual rainfall, and elevation as the dominant controls. Flow-R and RAMMS simulations reproduced representative runout patterns with κ = 0.74. Under CMIP6 SSP5-8.5, high-to-very-high susceptibility is projected to increase from 24.0% at baseline to 35.2% by 2050 and 41.6% by 2100. The multi-hazard assessment further indicates that 23.7% of the highway lies within high-to-very-high composite risk zones. The framework provides an explainable, climate-sensitive, and operationally transferable basis for landslide-risk reduction along high-relief transport corridors.

papers.title: Seismic–Tectonic Predictors of Landslide Susceptibility in the Western Himalayas: A Spatially Validated Machine Learning Assessment
papers.summary: Seismicity may contribute to regional slope instability in the Western Himalayas, but its incremental predictive value relative to a matched non-seismic baseline remains poorly quantified. This study assessed the regional contribution of seismic–tectonic predictors using 763 geocoded NASA Global Landslide Catalog reports from 2007–2017, 345 earthquakes of magnitude 5.5–7.6 from 1965–2016, mapped active faults, and hydrographic variables. Landslides were aggregated to a 0.25° grid, yielding 231 presence cells among 1,600 cells. Spatial block-permutation tests, nested five-fold spatial cross-validation, four classifiers, matched baseline comparisons, and SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP) were applied. Landslide-presence cells were closer to catalogued earthquakes than background cells (61.5 vs. 118.3 km; P = 0.0005) and had a higher energy-weighted seismicity index (2.323 vs. 2.003; P = 0.0015). Random forest achieved the strongest mean discrimination and calibration (ROC–AUC = 0.855 ± 0.027; PR–AUC = 0.489 ± 0.073; Brier score = 0.096 ± 0.004). Adding seismic–tectonic predictors increased random-forest ROC–AUC by 0.048 and reduced the Brier score by 0.014, although paired tests across five folds did not reach P < 0.05. The high and very high susceptibility classes occupied 16.5% of grid cells and contained 68.2% of catalogued events. Earthquake proximity, Gaussian earthquake density, and energy-weighted seismicity were the leading physical seismic predictors in SHAP analysis. These findings indicate useful regional seismic–tectonic predictive information but do not establish earthquake triggering or causation. Interpretation is limited by catalogue reporting bias, coarse mapping units, mixed magnitude scales, and unavailable terrain variables.

papers.title: From local hazards to connected climate risk: Compound extremes reveal a systemic blind spot
Between emergency and reconstruction: Territorial impacts and climate adaptation challenges after hurricane John in Guerrero
papers.summary: This chapter analyses the territorial, human, and socioeconomic impacts caused by Hurricane John (2024) in the state of Guerrero, with a particular focus on the municipalities of Acapulco and Coyuca de Benítez, within a context of increasing intensity and frequency of extreme hydrometeorological events. Using a territorial and comparative approach, the chapter examines the meteorological characteristics of the event, patterns of differentiated impacts, and the structural vulnerability conditions that shaped the magnitude of damage. The findings show that although Hurricane John exhibited lower wind intensity than previous events such as Hurricane Otis (2023), its extraordinary rainfall produced widespread impacts, including flooding, landslides, and significant socioeconomic disruptions, especially in rural and peri-urban areas. Furthermore, the assessment of post-disaster recovery processes reveals persistent structural gaps related to socioeconomic inequality, fragile urban infrastructure, and the limited integration of climate adaptation criteria into territorial planning. Overall, the chapter highlights the urgent need to move toward risk management and resilient reconstruction models that incorporate preventive, participatory, and territorially differentiated approaches, aimed at reducing future exposure and strengthening community adaptive capacity in the face of increasingly extreme climate scenarios.

papers.summary: "Monitoring and managing natural and human-induced disasters is vital for mitigating disaster risks and impacts due to increasing global climate variability, population growth, and rapid urbanization. Disasters such as earthquakes, landslides, and forest fires cause severe damage to human life and the natural environment. Their ability to spread over large areas and evolve rapidly often renders conventional field observation methods inadequate. In this context, remote sensing technologies offer significant advantages for disaster monitoring and analysis due to their capability to cover vast spatial areas and provide periodic data. Multispectral and high-resolution data obtained from satellite systems, unmanned aerial vehicles, and LiDAR technologies are effectively utilized for disaster detection, damage assessment, monitoring spatial-temporal dynamics, and the generation of risk maps. Furthermore, the increasing volume and complexity of remote sensing data have accelerated the integration of artificial intelligence, particularly deep learning and machine learning methods, into data analysis workflows. Convolutional neural networks, recurrent neural networks, long short-term memory, and recently developed transformer-based models offer advanced solutions for the automated detection, classification, and mapping of disasters from remotely sensed data. Through the integration of these technologies, applications such as post-earthquake damage assessment, landslide susceptibility mapping, early detection and monitoring of forest fires, and mucilage formation detection can be performed rapidly and effectively. papers.title: Yıkıntı Atıklarının Yönetiminde Saha Değerlendirmesi ve Önceliklendirme Yaklaşımı
papers.summary: "Natural disasters have the potential to generate large amounts of debris. The amount of waste generated in an instant can far exceed the amount that would have accumulated over years, overwhelming local waste management facilities beyond their capacity. This waste leads to deterioration of water and air quality, noise pollution, negative impacts on flora and fauna, visual pollution, and negative socioeconomic effects. If managed effectively, disaster waste can become a valuable resource in the recycling and reconstruction process, contributing to social and economic improvement. Following the two earthquakes on February 6, 2023, with epicenters in Pazarcık and Elbistan (Kahramanmaraş), field visits and various meetings with relevant institutions were conducted in Kahramanmaraş and Hatay provinces to support the development of disaster/waste management plans, and the data obtained was evaluated. Within the scope of this evaluation, the existing dumping sites in both provinces were also examined separately regarding the storage and recycling of demolition waste that is currently present and may be generated from future demolitions. These examinations, along with criteria such as dumping site area, distance to the nearest settlement, distance to pasture land, distance to forest land, distance to a stream, presence of landslide risk, topographical condition of the site, quality, geological structure, and vegetation, were used to prioritize the sites using a multicriteria decision-making method. As a result of the study, an alternative model was developed that can be used to determine the most suitable sites for the storage and recycling of demolition waste."

papers.summary: "This study examines the vulnerability and resilience of energy infrastructures to climate changeinduced disasters from the perspectives of energy security, supply continuity, disaster risk reduction and climate adaptation. papers.title: Edukasi dan Sosialisasi Kebencanaan Longsor Berbasis Komunitas untuk Penguatan Kelembagaan Komunitas Peduli Lingkungan Kampung Asbaken
papers.summary: Kampung Asbaken in Distrik Makbon, Kabupaten Sorong, faces recurring landslide risks due to steep topography, high rainfall, uncontrolled land clearing, and sparse deep-rooted vegetation. Compounding this vulnerability, local disaster literacy is limited, and the partner group, Komunitas Peduli Lingkungan Kampung Asbaken, lacks formal organizational structures and standard operating procedures (SOPs). This community engagement initiative aimed to enhance community-based landslide mitigation and strengthen local institutional capacity through training, participatory risk mapping, slope bioengineering, and evacuation-route marking. Involving 25 partner members and 30 residents across three workshops, the program evaluated knowledge gains using a 30-item pretest-posttest instrument. The mean knowledge score increased by 78.6%, rising from 48.7 (SD = 9.8) to 87.0 (SD = 6.9), while passing rates (score ≥ 70) improved from 20.0% to 90.0% (paired t = 17.4, p < .001). The partner group also formalized its organizational structure and mitigation SOPs. These results show that participatory education integrated with vegetative conservation and institutional capacity building effectively enhances rural disaster resilience.

papers.title: Integrated subsurface screening for bioengineering suitability and erosion control on a tropical cut slope
papers.summary: Tropical cut slopes are highly susceptible to erosion and shallow landslides because intense rainfall interacts with deeply weathered residual soils, yet bioengineering interventions are frequently designed without adequate subsurface characterization. This study aimed to conduct an integrated geological, geophysical, and geotechnical characterization of a tropical cut slope on the Kenny Hill Formation, Selangor, Malaysia, in order to evaluate its suitability for bioengineering. Field reconnaissance and weathering grade classification were combined with a two-dimensional electrical resistivity survey, soil penetration resistance, near surface moisture content, and erosion rate measurements collected across three vegetation coverage plots over 24 months. The slope was classified as Grade III to IV weathered metasedimentary rock with a sandy clay loam surface texture. Resistivity imaging identified a high resistivity, coarse textured near surface layer of 20,000 to 360,000 Ωm at 0 to 5 m depth, overlying a low resistivity, moisture affected zone of 300 to 800 Ωm at 5 to 14.8 m depth. The corresponding reduction in erosion rate confirms that the subsurface conditions identified through this integrated approach translate into measurable improvement in slope performance. papers.title: Shear Strength of Unsaturated Organic Clay across Natural Dry-Density Gradients from Landslide Sites in Bogor, Indonesia
papers.summary: Rainfall-induced landslides in tropical regions are closely linked to the loss of apparent cohesion as unsaturated soils approach saturation. This study examines how the apparent cohesion (c′) and internal friction angle (φ′) of unsaturated organic clay respond to variations in natural dry density (γd) across a range of degrees of saturation (Sr), using natural dry density values obtained from three actual landslide sites in Bogor, Indonesia, rather than from laboratory-compacted specimens. A total of 231 direct shear tests (3 sites × 7 specimens × 3 normal-stress levels × 3–4 repetitions) and 42 filter-paper tests (3 sites × 7 specimens × 2 repetitions) were performed on remolded specimens reconstituted to in-situ γd values at seven Sr levels. The results reveal four main findings. The three soils have very low and uniform air-entry values (1.52–2.09 kPa), so the suction contribution is lost soon after infiltration. Apparent cohesion does not decrease monotonically but peaks at intermediate saturation (44–56%), with peak values tiered according to density (10.60; 6.30; 4.69 kPa). c′ and φ′ respond to Sr through different mechanisms: c′ peaks while φ′ decreases monotonically. The cohesion advantage of the densest soil, prominent under moist conditions, vanishes near saturation, where the cohesion of the three densities converges to a nearly identical low value. A multiple linear regression model, c′ = 16.162·γd − 0.089·Sr − 5.076, is proposed as a practical estimator. These findings imply that initial density alone does not guarantee slope stability under heavy rainfall.

papers.title: 7269 Sayılı Kanun’dan Kaynaklanan Davalarda Genel Durum Analizi
papers.summary: This study examines the scope, fundamental provisions, and legal problems encountered in the implementation of Law No. 7269 on “Precautions to be Taken due to Disaster Affecting Public Life and Assistance to be Provided”, which aims to mitigate the effects of natural disasters and assist victims in Türkiye. Türkiye's location in an active earthquake zone increases the importance of this law. The law covers disaster types such as earthquakes, floods, and landslides, providing a comprehensive framework from pre-disaster measures to post-disaster aid. Among the most frequently encountered legal problems in practice are the criteria and review of disaster-stricken area declarations, appeal processes and judicial review concerning damage assessment reports, property uncertainties and inheritance issues in entitlement determination, value assessment in expropriation processes, and the administration's liability in compensation lawsuits. The annulment decision of the Constitutional Court of the Republic of Türkiye in 2023 regarding the inability of damage assessment reports to be subject to independent litigation is an important development. The study analyses these problems in light of judicial decisions and offers recommendations. Particularly, the necessity of establishing specialised judicial units and adopting effective procedural methods for the swift resolution of post- disaster legal disputes is emphasised. Additionally, the importance of raising disaster awareness and strengthening society's resilience against disasters is emphasised.

papers.title: Landslide-Resilient Hillside Housing: An Integrated System of Biopolymer Soil Treatment, Bio-Engineering, Micropiles and Siphon Drainage
papers.source: International Journal for Research in Applied Science and Engineering Technology
papers.summary: Landslides triggered by rain repeatedly destroy homes and livelihoods on the steep, weathered slopes of the Western Ghats and other high-rainfall hill regions. The usual remedies, retaining walls and deep foundations, tend to be costly, carbonheavy and awkward to build on remote ground, and they are normally applied one at a time even though most slope failures have several causes working together. This paper presents the concept and test plan for an integrated, low-impact housing system that deals with the soil, the slope surface, the foundation and the groundwater together. The soil is strengthened with xanthan gum, a microbial biopolymer that bonds particles and lowers permeability. The surface is protected by vetiver contour hedgerows and bamboo clumps whose roots hold the upper soil. The house stands on micropiles socketed below the potential slip surface, and a French drain with siphon pipes removes the water that raises pore pressure, without pumping. We review the literature behind each component, explain how the weakness of one measure (for example the water sensitivity of the biopolymer) is covered by another, and set out the methodology: site selection, soil characterisation to Indian Standards, a xanthan gum dosage programme, bio-engineering, micropile and drainage design, limit-equilibrium and finite-element stability analysis of four scenarios, and a reduced-scale rainfall model. Expected outcomes are stated qualitatively because no test data exist yet. Materials, a prototype work plan, a maintenance routine and future research needs are also listed.

papers.title: Rainfall-triggered railway earthwork instability: thresholds, hydrologic state and operational warning
papers.summary: Purpose Rainfall-triggered failures of railway embankments, cuttings and adjacent slopes are managed through rainfall thresholds, geotechnical assessment, monitoring and operating rules, but these elements are often evaluated separately. This review examines how the railway-earthwork evidence progresses from rainfall exposure through hydrologic state and physical response to operational action. Design/methodology/approach A structured critical evidence review was reconstructed from 596 screened records. Of 274 records advanced to the full-text stage, 105 verified full texts were assessed, 20 were excluded after full-text review, 169 had no verified full text and 85 studies were retained. Primary-objective coding was retained for description, while the principal synthesis used non-exclusive study-level coding of rainfall, hydrologic-state, response, operational and validation variables. Findings The retained corpus was predominantly railway-direct (83/85). Primary objectives were mechanism/stability response (29), threshold/risk prediction (28), mitigation/rehabilitation (15), monitoring/condition assessment (8) and operational warning/decision (5). Across all studies, stability/failure evidence appeared in 76, infiltration/seepage in 50 and deformation/displacement in 43. Thirty studies contained an explicit operational action, but only 9 of those reported validation, 3 reported non-failure controls, 1 reported a false-alarm metric, 1 a missed-event metric and none reported a lead-time metric. Practical implications For railway infrastructure managers, rainfall thresholds are best treated as network-level screening tools unless route-specific calibration and asset-state information support stronger decisions. Operational studies should report verified non-failure exposure, false alarms, missed events and usable lead time before a threshold, model or sensor output is relied upon for inspection, restriction, closure or resumption. Synthetic seismograms from r.avaflow landslide simulations
papers.summary: Flow models predict the motion of large landslides, but their predictions are rarely tested against records of a landslide as it moves. The force a landslide exerts on the Earth radiates long-period seismic waves that show how its mass accelerates. With synthetic seismograms of a simulated flow, these records can test the mechanics the simulation assumes, friction, failed mass, and failure sequence. We extend r.avaflow 4.0 to write the mass and first moments of the flow at every time step. The force is the negative second time derivative of these moments, corrected for added mass, convolved with Green's functions of a one-dimensional Earth, path-corrected with the GDM52 dispersion model or REM3D maps. On a plane, the force matches a rigid block within 1.2% after 3 s. The corrections raise the median correlation of records and synthetics for 20 earthquakes from 0.42 to 0.78 at 50–150 s and, for the 2026 Rasuwa–Trishuli landslide, from 0.17 to 0.43 at 30–150 s, more than eight friction settings change the fit. Uncorrected Green's functions underestimate the mass by a factor of 2.2. With them, the global seismic network can constrain the mechanics of landslides far from any instrument.

Landslide directionality reveals fault-influenced valley-slope geometry in the northern Xiaojiang Fault Zone
papers.summary: Regional landslide inventories commonly describe where landslides occur, but they rarely capture the directional organization of slope failure. We compiled a remote-sensing-derived geomorphic inventory with 3,442 landslides along the northern Xiaojiang Fault Zone, southeastern Tibetan Plateau, and defined the principal runout direction as the plan-view vector from the highest point along the rear boundary to the centroid of each landslide polygon. Circular statistics, fault-distance zoning and the angle between landslide direction and local fault strike (ΔF) were used to evaluate regional landslide directional patterns. Landslide directions show a clear multimodal distribution, dominated by east-southeast and west-southwest sectors. Directional concentration varies spatially, with the lowest value in the 0–1 km fault-distance zone (0.1149) and the highest value beyond 5 km (0.3898). ΔF is strongly concentrated at high angles, indicating that the principal direction vectors are not parallel to the fault. Instead, their directions are more consistent with local valley–slope geometry that may result from the combined effects of prolonged fault activity and fluvial downcutting. Principal runout direction therefore provides information complementary to conventional inventory metrics and offers a regional-scale indicator for examining tectonic–geomorphic organization in active-fault mountain landscapes.

papers.title: Geologic controls on spatial distribution and kinematics of Widespread Deep-seated Gravitational Slope Deformation in the Sawatch Range, Colorado
papers.summary: Deep-seated gravitational slope deformations (DSGSDs) are widespread landslide phenomena in many of Earth’s major mountain belts. However, in the continent-spanning Rocky Mountains, only 13 DSGSD have been previously reported. New mapping and characterization of Rocky Mountain DSGSD is thus needed to augment existing global inventories and constrain latent hazards to mountain communities and infrastructure. Here we compile the first range-scale DSGSD inventory in North America, focusing on the Sawatch Range of central Colorado. Through analysis of aerial imagery and lidar data, we identified 39 new DSGSD within a 2600 km2 area. Using detailed geomorphic mapping, field campaigns, and InSAR displacement analysis, we recorded critical attributes controlling DSGSD activity in the Sawatch Range. Most DSGSD creep down U-shaped valley flanks within Precambrian granite and gneiss. Previous orogenies, recent tectonics, and a history of extensive glaciations have conditioned slopes for DSGSD development, particularly on north-, northwest-, and west-facing aspects. Sawatch DSGSDs are generally less developed and extensive than their global counterparts, with active deformations exhibiting average velocities of around -1.0 cm/yr in Sentinel-1’s descending orbit look geometry. Site-specific surveys of the South Mt. Massive and Mt. Jones DSGSDs revealed that deformation styles vary across the range, with South Mt. Massive likely sliding on a deep rupture surface bounded by a normal fault, and Mt. Jones deforming by a combination of planar sliding along cataclinal foliation-parallel discontinuities and rotation. Sawatch DSGSDs deform under numerous mechanisms and provide unique morphologies not commonly found elsewhere in the world. Our results suggest the Rocky Mountains are likely to contain many more DSGSD than previously considered.

papers.title: Landslide Risk Mapping
Landslide impacts on people, infrastructure and the environment: a case study of Doda, Western Himalaya, India
papers.source: Journal of Ethnobiology and Environmental Research
papers.summary: Landslides are among the most common natural hazards in the hilly and mountainous regions of Jammu and Kashmir, India. The present study was conducted to assess the impacts of landslides across three selected sites in Doda district, Thathri, Kastigarh, and Pul Doda in 2026. Both primary and secondary data were collected during and after the monsoon season through field visits, direct observations, and structured questionnaire surveys administered to 151 respondents selected via purposive and random sampling techniques. Secondary data were compiled from peer-reviewed literature, government records, and official disaster reports. The study recorded 3 human fatalities and 18 injuries at Thathri, 1 fatality and 9 injuries at Kastigarh, and 0 fatalities and 13 injuries at Pul Doda. Respondents also reported extensive damage to residential houses, commercial shops, roads, vehicles, agricultural land, trees, and natural vegetation. Road blockages and transportation disruptions were the most widespread challenges across all three locations. Additionally, landslides contaminated local water sources, causing prolonged turbidity and water quality degradation. These findings demonstrate that landslides in Doda district generate severe socio-economic and environmental consequences. The results provide site-specific baseline evidence to support improved land-use planning, slope stabilization, road engineering and disaster risk reduction in the region. The study highlighted the need for effective landslide risk-reduction measures in Thathri, Kastigarh and Pul Doda. The slope should be stabilised through retaining walls, gabion structures, rock bolting and other suitable engineering techniques at vulnerable locations to reduce the future losses of life, property and environmental resources in Doda district.

papers.title: Uncovering Local Spatial Context via Multiscale Geographically Weighted Binomial Regression
papers.summary: This paper introduces a novel Multiscale Geographically Weighted Binomial Regression (MGWBR) model, extending the existing Multiscale Geographically Weighted Regression (MGWR) framework to accommodate binomial response variables. By integrating a Local Scoring Algorithm (LSA), the proposed MGWBR model accounts for spatial non-stationarity in binary outcomes and enables the estimation of covariate-specific bandwidths and localized parameter estimates. This approach addresses key limitations of traditional global binomial models and standard GWR models, which typically apply a single bandwidth and overlook the potential for spatially varying relationships across different predictors. To evaluate the performance of MGWBR, the model is applied to two simulated datasets and two empirical datasets: one on landslide occurrences in Clearwater national forest park and one on voting behavior in the Southeast U.S. during the 2020 presidential election. Results from both the simulated and real-world applications demonstrate that MGWBR provides improved model fit over traditional global binary regression models and effectively captures spatial heterogeneity in covariate effects, highlighting its potential as a robust tool for spatial analysis involving binary data.

papers.title: Numerical analysis of dynamics between debris flows and wave propagation using multi-layer shallow water equations
papers.source: Natural hazards and earth system sciences
papers.summary: Debris flows are destructive disasters that often cause casualties and property damage, particularly when occurring near residential areas. In reservoir basins, debris flows can reduce effective storage capacity by raising the dead storage level and generate waves that may induce overtopping or structural collapse. Previous numerical studies have applied three-dimensional (3D) hydrodynamics or smoothed particle hydrodynamics to analyze debris flow-induced waves. However, these studies focused on the direct inflow of soil masses into water, without accounting for erosion and entrainment processes. As a result, they have limitations in simulating debris generated in upland areas that undergo erosion and entrainment before entering reservoirs. To address this gap, we developed a one-dimensional (1D) multi-layer simulation model based on shallow water equations that explicitly considers erosion, entrainment, and deposition. The model was validated through theoretical analysis and a laboratory experiment, and applied to the 2020 Sanyang Reservoir collapse event in South Korea. Scenario-based simulations were performed under varying debris flow characteristics and reservoir water levels. The results demonstrate that debris flow momentum strongly correlates with the scale of generated waves, with maximum momentum serving as a reliable predictor of wave magnitude. This study offers a practical framework for assessing debris flow impacts on dam and reservoir safety.

papers.title: COHESION: a connectivity-based framework for evaluating landslide susceptibility, runout hazards, and hillslope–channel coupling
papers.source: Natural hazards and earth system sciences
papers.summary: Landslides hinder sustainable development in mountain regions by threatening livelihoods and damaging linear and water infrastructure. Susceptibility maps are widely used to identify landslide hazards, yet they usually omit hillslope connectivity. This is a critical shortcoming for mapping the magnitude of landslides, for identifying cascading hazards, and for understanding landslide contributions to fluvial sediment budgets. We introduce COHESION (COnnected HillslopE SusceptibIlity for slOpe failure and ruNout), a framework for coupling pixel-level susceptibility mapping approaches with connectivity analysis to identify downslope-connected landslide objects (LSOs), associated runout pathways and runout intersections with river networks. For the 7573 km 2 Kaligandaki Basin in Nepal, we base COHESION on a factor-of-safety assessment with probabilistic rainfall forcing and identify 1.06 million potential LSOs. Of these, 690 000 LSOs have nonzero precipitation-exceedance probabilities and cover 31.0 % of the basin. Precipitation-exceedance probabilities imply an annualized failure potential equivalent to 4.9 % of the basin area. Based on these probabilities, we propose that sediment mobilization from landsliding is constrained by soil-production and soil-mantle recovery rates rather than by triggering rainfall, a constraint hidden by typical susceptibility maps that do not account for failure volumes and probabilities. Considering runout pathways increases the mapped landslide-hazard footprint by 53.3 %. 29.7 % of buildings and 66.8 % of road segments are located on LSOs, while 20.7 % of buildings and 16.3 % of roads are on runout pathways. 35.3 % of LSOs connect to the river network, linking slope failures and river channels at more than 30 000 locations. Both results highlight the need to include connectivity and runout in geohazard screening and fluvial sediment budgets. COHESION's connectivity-based approach can improve the basin-scale screening of landslide hazard

papers.title: Seasonal biases induced by illumination changes and shadow casting in remote sensing derived glacier flow velocities
papers.summary: Sub-annual glacier surface velocity time series are receiving increasing attention as they provide critical information on subglacial hydrology, glacier and ice-sheet instabilities, and responses to external forcing. Regional-to-global scale datasets of glacier surface velocities are based on optical and/or SAR remote sensing images. They are now available worldwide in open access or on demand. Meanwhile, systematic seasonal errors (i.e., biases) induced by illumination changes and shadow casting have been reported in displacement time series derived from optical imagery for various landforms, such as landslides or dunes. The extent to which such biases affect glacier velocity maps remains poorly investigated. These biases may lead to misinterpretations of sub-annual velocity variations, for example, by amplifying or attenuating real seasonal signals or, in the worst case, producing artificial seasonal signals. Here, we characterize the amplitude and spatial distribution of seasonal biases in velocity maps derived from Sentinel-2 and Landsat 8/9 images. First, we compare GNSS velocity data measured on Argentière Glacier (French Alps) with three glacier surface flow velocity datasets derived from remote sensing images and post-processed using different state-of-the-art methodologies. We highlight a systematic overestimation of the seasonal amplitude among the different datasets, regardless of the post-processing strategies employed. Then, we assess the characteristics of this seasonal bias by analyzing velocities estimated over static areas at the scale of the Mont-Blanc Massif. Clear seasonal biases are observed on north-facing slopes, particularly on the northwestern aspect. The amplitude of this bias differs between the existing glacier surface velocity products, depending on the satellite images used and filters applied to the raw data. Across the Mont-Blanc Massif, the median value of this bias ranges from 7 to 80 m yr −1 on north-facing slopes for high to low l

papers.title: An operational risk assessment framework for landslide mitigation projects with a case study in the Three Gorges Reservoir Area
papers.summary: Large-scale landslide mitigation projects face complex environmental forces and long-term performance degradation. Existing risk assessments for landslide mitigation projects tend to focus primarily on structural limit states, often neglecting operational management factors and the distinction between risk probability and consequences. To address these gaps, this study develops an operational risk assessment framework integrating the Hierarchical Holographic Model (HHM), Best–Worst Method (BWM)–improved CRITIC game-theoretic weighting, and a bivariate normal cloud model. The system evaluates 18 indicators across four dimensions: hazard source, retaining structures, environment, and management. Critically, the bivariate cloud model simultaneously quantifies risk probability ( \(E{x}_{x}\) ) and consequence severity ( \(E{x}_{y}\) ). Applied to the Huangtupo landslide mitigation project in the Three Gorges Reservoir Area (TGRA), which has been in service for over 20 years, the framework yields an overall operational risk of Level III (General Risk) with a closeness similarity of \({\lambda}_{III}=0.6582\) . Cumulative displacement ( \({w}^{*}=0.1485\) ) and structural stress overload ( \({w}^{*}=0.1145\) ) are identified as primary physical drivers, exhibiting high consequence expectations ( \(E{x}_{y}=6.50\) and \(7.20\) ). The case study shows that an overall Level III classification can coexist with elevated risks associated with individual indicators, particularly cumulative displacement and stress overload. The framework brings these local concerns into the interpretation of project-level risk and provides a basis for setting monitoring and maintenance priorities.

papers.title: Integrating Geological Research and Environmental Monitoring in Mineral Extraction: A Critical Review of Frameworks, Technologies and Research Priorities
papers.source: International Journal of Scientific Research in Science and Technology
papers.summary: Mineral extraction is expanding to supply the materials required for the energy transition, while ore grades decline and the volumes of waste per unit of metal rise.These trends increase the environmental consequences of mining and make the traditional separation between geological investigation (exploration, resource modelling) and environmental monitoring (compliance sampling, post-hoc assessment) increasingly untenable.This review synthesises the literature on how geological knowledge and environmental monitoring can be integrated across the mine life cycle.We first summarise the geological controls on environmental risk, including deposit type, mineralogy, geochemical background and the prediction of acid and metalliferous drainage.We then review the monitoring toolbox: geochemical and hydrogeochemical sampling, portable analytical methods, geophysical imaging, optical and radar remote sensing, high-frequency sensors and DNA-based biomonitoring.Integration frameworks are examined, covering geoenvironmental models, geometallurgical and geoenvironmental block models, data-driven and machine-learning approaches, and early-warning systems for tailings and slope stability, illustrated with the Brumadinho, Tisza and Amazonian gold-mining cases.We discuss governance, datastandardisation and scale-mismatch barriers, and propose a research agenda centred on shared geo-environmental data infrastructure, uncertainty-aware prediction and closure-oriented monitoring design.The review argues that environmental performance is largely determined by geology that is already known, or knowable, at the exploration stage, and that monitoring is most effective when designed from the same geological model that guides extraction.

papers.title: Construction of the 2025 Gapyeong, Korea Landslide Inventory Map Using High- Resolution Satellite Imagery
papers.summary: This study presents a landslide inventory associated with the July 2025 heavy-rainfall event in Gapyeong-gun, South Korea, constructed by integrating optical satellite imagery, topographic information, and field observations. PlanetScope images with a spatial resolution of 3 m, acquired on July 12, 25, and 27, 2025, were visually interpreted to identify vegetation loss, exposed soil, and spatially connected sediment movement. Pre-event aerial orthophotos with a spatial resolution of 0.25 m and 1:5,000 digital topographic maps supported the examination of pre-existing land use and the manual identification of interpreted initiation points. Image re-examination and street-view screening reduced an initial set of 1,627 candidates to 737. Field investigation was conducted at 38 selected locations, and the findings were applied to candidates with similar characteristics, resulting in the exclusion of 131 points and a final inventory of 606 interpreted landslide initiation points. A 10 m digital elevation model was generated by linear triangulated irregular network interpolation of 5 m interval contours. Elevation, slope, and aspect values were extracted at the inventory points, and geographic coordinates were recorded in WGS84. The resulting KML point dataset documents the mapped distribution of landslide initiation locations associated with the event and provides spatial information for subsequent environmental analysis, landslide susceptibility studies, and targeted follow-up surveys.

The record includes Python scripts for data download, predictor construction, case-control sampling, spatial block cross-validation, XGBoost/random forest/logistic regression, SHAP attribution, map prediction and figures; derived model metrics, bootstrap confidence intervals, cross-inventory predictions, spatial folds, label geometry and sensitivity analyses; and the exact values plotted in Figures 1-4. Raw public datasets (DOGAMI SLIDO, USGS 3DEP, ESA WorldCover, gridMET, OpenStreetMap, USGS SGMC) are not redistributed; DATA_SOURCES.md lists their endpoints, access date and licences, and the download scripts are included. Main findings: same-inventory AUC is similar for the two representations (0.779 point vs 0.792 deposit), but cross-inventory transfer falls to 0.593 (point to deposit) and 0.608 (deposit to point), and the two final maps share only 34.5% of their top-20% area (Spearman rho = 0.36). A size-matched deposit model reproduces the deposit result, so the contrast is not a sample-size artefact. Released under CC BY 4.0. papers.title: Environmental drivers of deforming bedrock landslides in southern Alaska
papers.summary: Large moving bedrock subaerial landslides pose considerable hazards to people, infrastructure, and environments if they fail rapidly and run out over land or into water bodies and produce damaging waves. Identification of these features across the landscape can determine physiographic and environmental factors that influence landslide occurrence, aiding landslide hazard and risk assessments. To accomplish this, we apply persistent scatterer interferometric synthetic aperture radar (PSInSAR) methods with three years of Sentinel−1 data (2019 − 2021) to map 239 deforming bedrock landslides across 617,000 km 2 of southern Alaska and describe their physiographic setting. Identified landslides range in volume from approximately 0.4–1860 million cubic meters. The landslides are predominantly in sedimentary rock located on warmer south-facing slopes, and may be particularly sensitive to changes in hydrologic, thermal, and permafrost conditions that affect slope stability. Frequency-ratio analysis demonstrates that the identified landslides have a positive association with transient permafrost conditions and are 3.6 times more likely to occur within 2 km of a glacier, emphasizing the influence of ongoing cryosphere degradation on rock slope stability. Climate projections indicate substantial reductions in near-surface permafrost and glaciers over the next half century, which will modify landslide susceptibility throughout southern Alaska. The new regional inventory of hundreds of recently deforming bedrock landslides can help to refine susceptibility assessments and prioritize future analyses and risk mitigation efforts in Alaska.

papers.title: Unfolding the preconditioning role of root-zone soil moisture in rainfall-driven shallow landslides in the northeastern Himalayas
papers.summary: Moisture-driven landslides (MDLs) are a recurring hazard in the Northeastern Himalayas (NEH) during the southwest monsoon, where extreme rainfall, sustained wetness, and steep terrain combine to destabilize slopes. However, the compound influence of triggering rainfall, antecedent precipitation, and regional wetness, described by rootzone saturation on landslide frequency, remains unexplored. Using 611 MDLs from 21 sites (2007–2021), we show that compound interactions among moisture drivers substantially amplify landslide hazards than solely relying on rainfall-driven triggers. Triggering rainfall is the dominant driver overall, but ~41% (7 of 17) of sites with ≥15 landslides show strong antecedent moisture control. MDL likelihood conditioned on rainfall compounded with lag-1 root-zone-soil moisture exceeds the corresponding rainfall-only likelihood across 17 of the 18 threshold ranges (from 5th–10th percentiles to >90th percentile), with at-site amplification approaching twofold. Of the 27 large MDLs analyzed across 15 sites, 11 events show joint exceedance probabilities ≤10% when interdependencies among multiple drivers are considered, compared with solely rainfall-based landslide triggers, indicating a potential for predecessor compounding drivers in controlling landslides in this region. Further, validation indicates improved landslide predictability when predecessor moisture information (antecedent precipitation and rootzone saturation) is incorporated, although longer records are required to reduce uncertainty associated with prediction.

papers.summary: Background: The Pesisir Barat corridor sustains more than 1,200 micro-enterprises whose logistics are exposed to perishable-goods spoilage and frequent geohazard events. Objectives: To construct a juridical-digital twin that concurrently optimises multimodal routing, guarantees hygienic handling, and embeds enforceable contractual triggers grounded in the Indonesian Civil Code. Methods: A mixed-integer linear programming (MILP) model minimises total logistics cost-including transport, demurrage, spoilage, and breach penalties-subject to capacity, vessel-size, and geohazard constraints (BMKG-reported wave height >=2.5 m, landslide probability >=0.15). Spoilage is modelled by an Arrhenius-type degradation function S(t)=S0·exp[k(T-Tref)t] with parameters calibrated from a 2024 survey of 312 vendors. Real-time sensor readings are recorded on a permissioned blockchain hygiene ledger; cryptographic hashes of breach events activate smart-contract clauses that impose liquidated damages proportional to the MILP-derived penalty term P_breach. Contractual provisions operationalise Articles 1243, 1244, 1338, and 1320 of the Indonesian Civil Code, mandating carrier insurance at 150 % of shipment value and a 60/40 risk-sharing formula for force-majeure. Results: Empirical simulation demonstrates a 12.3 % reduction in total logistics cost and a 27.8 % decline in spoilage relative to a baseline without digital-legal integration. Conclusion: The synergistic fusion of rigorous logistics optimisation, blockchain traceability, and codified legal triggers yields a resilient, cost-effective supply-chain framework for micro-enterprises operating in hazard-prone coastal regions. papers.title: Climate Change, Human Displacement and Mobility Governance in Cameroon: A Critical Review of Environmental Drivers, Vulnerability and Policy Responses
papers.source: Journal of Geography Environment and Earth Science International
papers.summary: Cameroon combines a steep climatic gradient, from the Sudano-Sahelian plains of the Lake Chad Basin to the humid Atlantic littoral, with some of the largest and most protracted displacement crises in Central Africa. Floods, droughts, rain-triggered landslides, coastal erosion and urban inundation already move people within the country, yet these movements unfold alongside insurgency, separatist conflict and intercommunal violence that dominate humanitarian accounting. This critical narrative review examines how climate-related displacement and wider climate mobilities in Cameroon have been conceptualised, evidenced and governed, and evaluates the strength of the claims that link climate change to displacement in the country. Peer-reviewed literature, francophone scholarship and authoritative institutional documents published between 2009 and 2026 were identified through multidisciplinary open scholarly databases, a regional open archive, institutional repositories and citation chasing, and were appraised qualitatively for relevance, methodological transparency, analytical depth, credibility and governance contribution. The synthesis shows that hazard science for Cameroon has advanced considerably, particularly for extreme rainfall, urban flooding and coastal change, whereas mobility outcomes are seldom measured directly. Claims that climate change drives displacement around Lake Chad and in the Logone floodplain rest more on policy narratives than on demonstrated causal pathways, and the best available evidence points to climate variability acting through land, water, political and security conditions rather than as an independent driver. Pastoral mobility, seasonal migration and rural–urban movement emerge as long-standing adaptive repertoires that are increasingly constrained by insecurity, land pressure and sedentarist policy. papers.title: Harnessing Geospatial Intelligence for Hurricane, Earthquake Response, and Recovery
papers.summary: Geohazards such as hurricanes, volcanic eruptions, earthquakes, tsunamis, landslides, and subsidence continue to threaten lives, infrastructure, ecosystems, and economic stability across tectonically and climatically vulnerable regions. This chapter presents geospatial intelligence as an integrated framework that combines remote sensing, Geographic Information Systems, Interferometric Synthetic Aperture Radar, Global Navigation Satellite System and Global Positioning System observations, Light Detection and Ranging, thermal infrared imagery, data from ground seismological networks, distributed acoustic sensing, field geology, and historical disaster records. This chapter highlights how these datasets help to improve the detection of ground deformation, geotectonic dynamics around active faults, volcanic unrest, storm surge exposure, coastal flooding, slope instability, and post-disaster damage. Particular attention is given to the growing role of artificial intelligence, machine learning, deep learning, and geospatial artificial intelligence applications in extracting weak signals from large and noisy geospatial datasets. Methods such as convolutional neural networks, recurrent neural networks, transformer models, automated seismic phase picking, landslide segmentation, deformation detection, and hurricane surge prediction are discussed as tools for improving hazard forecasting and emergency decision-making. This chapter also emphasizes that effective AI applications must remain grounded in geophysical, geological, and hydrodynamic understanding rather than relying only on statistical pattern recognition. By integrating multi-source observations with physically informed modelling, geospatial intelligence supports early warning, risk mapping, infrastructure vulnerability assessment, evacuation planning, and disaster recovery. papers.summary: Landslides have not only caused significant economic losses but also claimed several lives. Though the impacts of this extreme event are felt worldwide, they are most concentrated in Asia, South America and Africa. This chapter presents geospatial techniques for landslide hazard and susceptibility mapping, ranging from heuristic and statistical methods to advanced machine learning approaches. The collection of remote sensing data was explored using optical, synthetic aperture radar, light detection and ranging and unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV) platforms, along with data fusion methods to address gaps in datasets. Some case studies of the application of the techniques have been documented for the Himalayas, the Andes, the European Alps, the Rocky Mountains, the East African Rift, Southeast Asia and the Loess Plateau. The model validation, uncertainty quantification, explainable artificial intelligence (AI) and ethical considerations were all addressed. Static hazard maps have been transformed into dynamic ones for early warning systems by synthesising AI-based spatial predictions with real-time monitoring, enabling policy implementation through proper land-use planning, climate adaptation and transboundary cooperation.

papers.title: ArcticDEM Workbench for Traceable Multitemporal Elevation Change Analysis
papers.summary: Repeat ArcticDEM (Arctic Digital Elevation Model) strips can reveal rapid surface-height changes, but comparing acquisitions and registration methods requires fixed locations, consistent screening and recoverable processing decisions. ArcticDEM Workbench v0.11.1 is a Python desktop and command-line application that links ArcticDEM discovery, native-resolution quality masking, co-registration, temporal-network diagnostics and elevation-change reporting. Its primary engineering contribution is the retention of acquisition identities, named spatial objects, configuration records and shared evaluation masks across methods and sessions, rather than a new universal registration estimator. We describe the released implementation, 104 regression checks on each of Windows and Ubuntu, and an offline known-change experiment that recovered a median elevation difference of −8.004 m in a patch prescribed −8 m. A four-epoch application to the 2017 Kinnikinnick landslide, Alaska, uses common reference and target masks and compares an event-step estimate with a published ArcticDEM-derived product. On 6008 shared source pixels, the locally area-corrected net surface-lowering integral was 368.47 × 103 m3 for joint-gradient registration and 366.38 × 103 m3 for the published product; pixelwise agreement did not follow the same ranking. The example demonstrates why temporal definitions, area conventions and common valid support must accompany elevation-change statistics. The software is scoped to area-limited studies, with explicit memory and observation-count limits.

papers.summary: Loess landslides exhibit strong spatial heterogeneity and complex rainfall responses, making their evolution difficult to characterize from one-dimensional deformation observations alone. This study investigates the Li-Kan Highway landslide on the right bank of the Lijiaxia Reservoir, China, by integrating ascending- and descending-track time-series InSAR, aspect-parallel flow (APF) constrained three-dimensional deformation reconstruction, the Comprehensive Standardized Deformation Index (CSDI), wavelet-based rainfall-response analysis, and Massflow numerical simulation. The reconstructed deformation field shows that the landslide is dominated by northeastward horizontal motion, while local sectors exhibit distinct movement directions and deformation components, indicating multiple kinematic units. Along the approximately 2 km P–P′ profile, the north–south, east–west, and vertical deformation–velocity components exhibit spatially variable patterns, consistent with heterogeneous slope kinematics. Principal component analysis shows that the first two components explain 85.6% of the total variance, summarizing the spatial variability. CSDI analysis of representative points P1–P3 reveals asynchronous deformation activity: P1 is mainly active in autumn 2018, P2 shows enhanced activity in 2019 and spring–summer 2020, and P3 exhibits a weaker local increase around mid-2021. In particular, the 2020 response at P2 is interpreted as a local kinematic adjustment rather than synchronous acceleration of the entire slope. Because no overall failure occurred during the observation period, CSDI-defined Stage III is treated as enhanced deformation activity rather than a direct failure criterion. Continuous wavelet transform and time-lag cross-correlation indicate significant rainfall-related temporal responses, with deformation lagging rainfall by approximately 12, 108, and 36 days at P1, P2, and P3, respectively. papers.title: Computer Vision Techniques for Remote Sensing, Hazard Detection, and Predictive Modelling
papers.summary: The recent progress in computer vision has made it much easier to extract meaningful insights from remote sensing data for environmental risk assessment. In this chapter, a unified framework is presented that brings together transformer-based feature learning, multimodal data fusion, and self-supervised techniques to improve both hazard detection and prediction. The method integrates optical, synthetic aperture radar (SAR), and thermal unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV) imagery within a single spatiotemporal structure, allowing data from different sources and resolutions to be analysed in a consistent way. This makes it more effective in identifying events such as floods, wildfires, landslides, and other surface-related hazards. Tests carried out on multiple multi-sensor datasets show clear improvements over existing approaches. The framework achieves a 14% to 22% increase in detection accuracy, reduces false alarms by 18%, and extends the forecasting lead time by up to 30%. It also performs reliably across different types of terrain and remains stable even when the input data is noisy or incomplete. Taken together, these results demonstrate the practical value of the approach for real-time monitoring, early warning systems, and informed decision-making in managing climate-related risks.

papers.title: Geospatial Risk Assessment for Disaster Management
papers.summary: Across the African continent, the consequences of natural disasters such as floods that erase farmlands overnight, earthquakes that crumble poorly built housing, landslides triggered by deforested slopes are rarely accidental. They reflect decades of unmanaged exposure and entrenched vulnerability. This chapter investigates the role of geospatial technologies and artificial intelligence (AI) in transforming how disaster risk is understood, mapped, and acted upon. Grounded in the Sendai Framework’s conceptual architecture of hazard, exposure, vulnerability, and resilience, it traces the journey from conventional Geographic Information System-based risk mapping toward AI-powered spatial analytics capable of handling satellite streams, environmental sensor feeds, and citizen-generated data at unprecedented scale and speed. This chapter draws on African examples from Nigeria’s recurrent flood crises to Freetown’s landslide tragedy to demonstrate both the operational gains these tools offer and the structural limitations that constrain their impact, including data scarcity, algorithmic bias, and governance deficits. Special attention is given to the September 2024 Alau Dam collapse and Maiduguri floods as a Nigerian case study illustrating both geospatial response capacity and early warning gaps. This chapter concludes with a forward-looking discussion of real-time analytics, climate-integrated risk modelling, and the irreplaceable role of community knowledge and human judgement.

papers.title: Meshfree simulation of hydrodynamic interactions among multiple colliding rigid bodies with complex geometries
papers.summary: A two-way coupling framework is developed for fluid--rigid-body interactions involving collisions among multiple bodies with complex geometries. The framework combines stabilized least squares moving particle semi-implicit (LSMPS) and distance-potential discrete element method (DEM) formulations through an immersed boundary (IB) treatment. Hydrodynamic forces and torques are determined from velocity corrections at surface IB points. To improve coupling accuracy, a two-level iterative procedure coordinates IB enforcement, pressure projection, and rigid-body motion to reduce interface and incompressibility residuals. Fluid particles covered by moving solids remain active in the Navier--Stokes and pressure-projection calculations. This continuous particle cloud alleviates the loss of numerical support in closing gaps. Analytical, numerical, and experimental comparisons in three two-dimensional benchmarks assess the overall coupled response through viscous angular-momentum transfer, wake-mediated drafting and tumbling, and wave generation by a sliding rigid body. Two-dimensional applications to multi-block sedimentation and submerged landslide impact examine discharge between moving bodies, collision-driven momentum redistribution, recirculation, collapse, and deposition. Global energy and kinematic diagnostics supplement the flow-field comparisons. The results demonstrate continued calculation through complex multi-body motion without interpreting numerical robustness as physical resolution of sub-spacing gaps.

papers.title: Quality-screened GNSS benchmarking finds limited distance-graph gains for landslide displacement forecasting
papers.summary: Ground-based Global Navigation Satellite System (GNSS) networks can track landslide motion at hourly resolution, but missing records and uneven station quality complicate multi-station forecasting. We used a long-term Huangtupo landslide monitoring record to test whether a distance-graph prior improves displacement-increment forecasts after retrospective station admission. Shared temporal baselines and graph models were trained with identical inputs, rolling-origin splits, and random seeds. The Shared GRU achieved a mean absolute error of 0.2755 mm, slightly below 0.2774 mm for the Graph-fusion GRU; this 0.0019 mm difference is much smaller than the 0.1 mm record resolution and estimated increment-noise scale. Expanding the quality-screened node set narrowed the branch gap but did not reverse the ranking, and the small early 12 h gap did not persist in later folds. Leave-one-station-out, topology, and coherence controls showed heterogeneous station effects but no stable evidence that admission eligibility or distance proximity ordered graph-specific predictive value. A secondary GNSS/InSAR correspondence screen also found no station clearly separated from stable-ground and permutation controls. For this single slope, retrospectively admitted node set, and distance-graph protocol, the results support quality-screened benchmarking before deploying graph-based landslide forecasting models.

papers.title: Feature-based clustering of DInSAR time series to unveil complex landslide kinematic patterns
papers.summary: Differential Interferometric Synthetic Aperture Radar (DInSAR) data processing generates displacement time series widely used for landslide mapping and monitoring. In many cases, displacement time series exhibit non-linear behaviour, which limits the applicability of conventional velocity-based classifications for detecting and interpreting landslide kinematics. Time series clustering has recently been introduced to identify displacement patterns. However, existing workflows often divide time series into a few and simple displacement styles, failing to discriminate between behaviours associated with gradual to abrupt velocity changes. This study investigates a clustering framework to unveil unknown displacement patterns in a large time series dataset. It exploits data dimensionality reduction by feature extraction to improve cluster mapping. A set of statistical features is proposed to describe different time series characteristics (e.g. average velocity, timing of changepoint, linear trend, and curvature), which is potentially useful for cluster-based classification of any DInSAR dataset. This study uses COSMO-SkyMed satellite data and tests the method over the historical town of Civitacampomarano (southern Italy), where a destructive landslide occurred in March 2017, causing the evacuation of a neighbourhood. Clustering helps identify displacement patterns and slope sectors requiring further investigation and distinguish between long-term ground instabilities and the ones potentially triggered by critical rainfall events or earthquakes. Particularly, the cluster of the March 2017 landslide was isolated, helping to constrain its spatial extent and investigate its triggering factors.

papers.title: A multi-variable threshold approach to landslide prediction: integrating rainfall, soil moisture, and soil texture in Indonesia
papers.summary: Landslides are one of the most devastating hazards globally, including in Indonesia. To reduce casualties, Indonesia has established the Blueprint of Indonesian Landslide Early Warning System (BILEWS). This system currently relies on rainfall-induced landslide thresholds for issuing the warning signals derived from historical landslide occurrences in Java, Sumatra, and Kalimantan Islands. However, landslide occurrence is strongly influenced not only by rainfall but also by antecedent soil moisture conditions and soil characteristics. Therefore, BILEWS still faces technical challenges in accurately predicting landslides, especially in Sulawesi and Papua Islands, where Java’s threshold is applied there. This study aims to enhance the existing rainfall thresholds and incorporate soil moisture into a multi-variable threshold framework. Specifically, rainfall thresholds, soil moisture thresholds, and the combination of rainfall-soil moisture thresholds are developed. In addition, the relationship between soil moisture and landslide occurrence is evaluated across different soil textures. The results indicate that the optimal thresholds vary across islands. The existing rainfall thresholds yield the highest performance in Java and the Sumatra Islands with Youden Index of 0.545 and 0.740, respectively. In Sulawesi Island, the best performed threshold is the newly developed rainfall threshold with a Youden Index of 0.477. The rainfall-soil moisture thresholds show optimum performance for Kalimantan (0.465) and Papua (0.458) Islands. Furthermore, soil moisture significantly affects landslide risks in sandy clay loam and loam soil textures. Developing thresholds based on significant soil textures improves the performance of landslide prediction.

Monitoring indicated progressively wetter conditions prior to failure, with soil moisture approaching saturation and matric suction decreasing across the intervention. Model simulations reproduced the observed shallow failure mechanism and predicted instability on 23 December 2022, two days before the reported intervention failure. The observed failure was only predicted for the shallow slip surface under fallow and critical groundwater scenarios. In contrast, for deeper slip surfaces, elevated groundwater levels resulted in instability irrespective of the presence of vegetation cover. papers.title: Climate Change and Vulnerability
papers.summary: The effect of climate change on health-related variables remains an underexplored area. This paper discusses the effect of climatic change on factors relating to physiological and psychological health, examines the channels through which climate variation influences human health, and briefly explains the vulnerabilities and adaptive measures associated with the issue. Particular emphasis is placed on Catastrophic Health Care Expenditure (CHE). The paper addresses the relationship between climatic change and CHE in the Kerala context, given that CHE drives individuals and households into poverty — an important dimension of vulnerability. Kerala is selected for this study due to its combination of high morbidity and its recent experience of severe climatic and geological events, such as floods and landslides. The paper is organised into the following parts: the first examines the different dimensions of climatic change and its implications for health, drawing on the available literature; the second reviews the Kerala scenario with respect to the link between healthcare and climate change; the paper then undertakes an exploratory analysis of the connection between climatic change and CHE in Kerala, drawing on insights from the first section, and concludes with observations on the probable impact of climate change on catastrophic out-of-pocket health expenditure.

papers.title: Mountain carbon budgets miss cryosphere hazard events
papers.summary: Warming is destabilizing the mountain cryosphere and triggering more frequent hazard events. These hazards mobilize large stores of carbon as well as rock, ice and water. Yet mountain carbon budgets largely overlook this flux, because routine monitoring rarely operates at the time, location and resolution that hazard events demand. We argue that cryosphere hazards should be treated as carbon events and set out how to close the gap. Here, cryosphere hazard events are mass movements in glacial and permafrost terrain whose onset is abrupt relative to gradual degradation, together with the cascades they trigger (Ding et al., 2021;Zhang et al., 2025). papers.title: Evaluation of Stage IV and MRMS Quantitative Precipitation Estimates over Puerto Rico across Rainfall Intensity Categories and Geographic Regions
papers.summary: Reliable Quantitative Precipitation Estimation (QPE) is essential for flood forecasting, landslide monitoring, and water resource management in hazard-prone tropical environments. This study evaluates two widely used QPE products, Stage IV and the Multi-Radar Multi-Sensor (MRMS) system at 1-km and 4-km spatial resolutions over Puerto Rico using hourly rain gauge observations from October 2020 to November 2023. A distance-based IDW method was applied to extract QPE values at gauge locations, and its sensitivity relative to conventional nearest-pixel matching was evaluated. The evaluation encompassed both unconditional and percentile-based conditional assessments across four precipitation intensity categories (light, moderate, heavy, and extreme) and six geographic regions. Results show that MRMS-1km consistently outperforms Stage IV and MRMS-4km across most metrics, with higher Pearson correlation coefficients (PCC) and lower root mean square error (RMSE), particularly for moderate to extreme precipitation. All products exhibit notably reduced skill for light precipitation. Spatially, the eastern and metro zones yield the lowest errors, while the western, southern, and northern zones show higher RMSE, partly attributed to greater radar distance and complex terrain. The RMSE–distance relationship is nonlinear for light and moderate rainfall, weakening under extreme conditions where attenuation and vertical reflectivity effects become dominant. Geographically weighted regression (GWR) analysis reveals spatially heterogeneous distance–error relationships, most pronounced for MRMS-1km over the central mountainous region. These findings provide actionable guidance for QPE product selection in hydrologic applications and highlight priority areas for targeted gauge-based correction in complex tropical island terrain.

papers.title: Debris-flow (torrent) cones triggered by extreme rainfall during the June 2020 flash-flood event in the Eastern Polish Flysch Carpathians
papers.summary: The immediate cause of debris-flow cones formation was the short-lived but intense rainfall on 26 June 2020, which affected catchments of small rivers (ranging from several dozen to 200 km2) located in the Carpathian Foothills (300–500 m a.s.l.). The issue of debris-flow cones formation is presented in the context of the geomorphological effects of flash floods in selected catchments of the middle San River basin during the June 2020 events. Torrential cones were formed by debris-mud flows in forested, steeply inclined (>10%) V-shaped valleys (with catchment areas below 1.5 km−2). Valley incision reached approximately 1.0–1.5 m. Based on the type and grain size of the deposited material, three cone types were distinguished: 1) larger debris cones containing rock blocks up to 90 cm in diameter, 2) smaller silty-debris cones, composed mainly of clasts and soil-derived sands with a minor share of coarse debris, and 3) silty-sandy fan deltas, whose accumulation resulted from a temporary blockage of flow. The triggering of debris flows and the formation of torrential cones require hourly rainfall intensities of at least 40–50 mm (daily total around 80 mm). An important factor in the initiation of debris and mud flows is the antecedent phase preceding the main rainfall event. In this case, 11 days with rainfall before the downpour on 26 June 2020, led to the saturation of surface deposits, which facilitated the activation of flows and the transport of debris-water masses within the valleys.

papers.title: Climate Vulnerability to Food Security in a Non-Agrarian Buffer City of Indonesia's New Capital: A Descriptive Study of Balikpapan City
papers.summary: Balikpapan, a coastal, non-agrarian city serving as the primary logistics and residential hub supporting Indonesia's new capital (Ibu Kota Nusantara, IKN), faces two interconnected challenges: increasing exposure to climate-related hazards and a food system that relies heavily on external supplies for nearly all strategic commodities. This study examines the vulnerability of Balikpapan's food security to climate change using the exposure–sensitivity–adaptive capacity framework, supported by a primary survey of food loss and waste (FLW) across 25 food-service units (6 hotels and 19 government-operated Nutrition Fulfillment Service Units, Satuan Pelayanan Pemenuhan Gizi [SPPG]) and secondary data from the city's 2025–2029 Regional Food and Nutrition Action Plan (Rencana Aksi Daerah Pangan dan Gizi, RAD-PG). The findings reveal that 93 landslides, 25 floods, 31 vegetation fires, and two extreme weather events were recorded in 2024, alongside a decline in the harvested paddy area from 66 to 23 hectares between 2020 and 2024. Local production met only approximately 1.94% of the demand for 12 strategic food commodities. Total FLW across the surveyed units reached 1,152.85 kilograms per day, with uneaten food portions returned by recipients accounting for the largest share (52.55%). A five-dimensional gap analysis comparing current conditions with the 2029 targets identifies governance and investment in climate-resilient local food systems as the areas with the largest gaps. Based on these findings, the study proposes five strategic directions for future action, building on the existing social forestry-based Integrated Area Development program.

A Three-Party Evolutionary Game in a Multi-Actor Emergency Management Feedback System
papers.summary: Emergency management is a multi-actor feedback system spanning risk identification, response activation, rescue assurance, and recovery arrangements. Evolving disaster pressure requires government, professional media, and networked publics to coordinate resource dispatch, action information, and demand response within a limited response window. Using the Pengshui landslide as a case, this study integrates microblog activity records, event-process nodes, and public numerical resource records to develop a three-party evolutionary game and calibrate its parameters against the observed case paths. Numerical scenario comparisons examine the dynamic feedback between substantive government response, media verification and explanation, public cooperative response, and the five states of usable response capacity, information certainty, social response pressure, network-expression pressure, and response credibility. Delivered resources, distribution, and service outcomes build response capacity, while public progress disclosure supports media verification and public action. Media verification of risk scope, resource destinations, and assurance progress improves information certainty; public evacuation support, demand reporting, and verified-information forwarding bring field needs into dispatch and explanation. In the recovery limit, as exogenous disaster pressure tends to zero, the collaborative-recovery point is locally asymptotically stable in all 13 primary scenarios. Starting from the Pengshui initial conditions under the time-varying exogenous disaster-pressure path, the scenarios differ in the timing and persistence of cooperation over the finite simulation window. The study represents resource assurance, information governance, and public collaboration as mutually dependent components of an emergency collaboration system and clarifies their dynamic feedback linkage.

Rehabilitation of Reinforced Concrete Beams Exposed to Loss of Flexural Strength by Embedded Steel Bars with Numerically Confinement Steel Plate
papers.summary: A comprehensive nonlinear finite element analysis was conducted to investigate the rehabilitation of reinforced concrete beams that have suffered a significant loss of flexural strength. The proposed rehabilitation strategy integrates near-surface-mounted (NSM) embedded steel bars with externally bonded (EB) steel plate confinement, offering a cost-effective and mechanically reliable alternative to fiber-reinforced polymer (FRP)-based methods. Numerical simulations in ABAQUS assessed the effects of key parameters, including the number, length, and equivalent area of embedded steel bars, the confinement length of steel plates, the presence or absence of lap splices, the loading type, and the concrete compressive strength. Model validation against experimental data showed close agreement in ultimate load, deflection, and load–deflection response. Results demonstrated that NSM steel bars partially restored flexural capacity, while the addition of confinement steel plates substantially improved both strength recovery and deformability. Increased confinement length and continuous main reinforcement were especially effective, resulting in load capacities surpassing those of undamaged control beams. Repeated loading negatively impacted NSM-only systems, whereas NSM–EB rehabilitation achieved significant load recovery. Higher concrete compressive strength further enhanced load recovery but reduced deformation capacity. These findings establish that the combined application of embedded steel bars and confinement steel plates is an efficient repairing strategy for damaged RC beams.

papers.title: Calcination-Induced Structural Evolution of Nickel Phosphate and Its Impact on Charge-Storage Kinetics
papers.summary: Supercapattery performance is governed by the intrinsic properties of its electrode materials, particularly the relationship between microstructure and electrochemical behaviour. In a previous study, amorphous nickel phosphate (NP) has shown superior electrochemical performance as a battery-type electrode despite the common expectation that crystalline materials perform better in electrochemical response. In this work, NP was synthesized via a sonochemical route and its crystallinity was modulated by varying calcination temperatures. At lower calcination temperatures (300–600 ºC), NPs remain predominantly amorphous but turn crystalline when higher temperatures are applied. The thermal treatment also influenced the degree of hydration, particle morphology and pore structure. Among all temperatures, NP calcined at lower temperatures delivered the higher specific capacity and showed predominantly diffusion-influenced Faradaic kinetics. In contrast, NP calcined at higher temperatures showed lower specific capacity, but a stronger surface-control contribution to charge storage. These findings demonstrate that a high degree of crystallinity does not necessarily guarantee high charge-storage capacity and reveal a clear trade-off between active-site utilization and reaction kinetics during the amorphous to crystalline evolution of NP.
