Groundwater and surface water quality under urbanization pressure: A water quality index assessment in Siliguri Planning Area, India
papers.summary: Safe drinking water and sustainable water resource management require routine evaluations of groundwater and surface water quality. Rapidly expanding urban areas depend heavily upon these crucial assessments. Consequently, the spatial distribution of water quality parameters within the Siliguri Planning Area of West Bengal, India, was evaluated in this work. The Water Quality Index (WQI) was also calculated for both groundwater and surface water resources. The Weighted Arithmetic Water Quality Index method categorized the overall condition of these hydrological resources. A spectrum ranging from good to very poor conditions (WQI ranging from 34.02 to 182.30) defines the current groundwater quality. Elevated nitrate (up to 118 mg/L), iron (0.55 mg/L), and potassium concentrations heavily contaminate the central and southeastern urban zones. Strong positive relationships among nitrate, sodium, and sulphate (r > 0.90) were identified through correlation analysis. Human-driven pollution from agricultural runoff and domestic sewage is clearly indicated by these substantial linkages. Notable spatial variation characterized the surface water quality, with SWQI scores fluctuating between 12 and 76.97. Elevated BOD, TDS, and chloride concentrations drove a progressive deterioration along the urban corridors of the Mahananda River. Conversely, relatively healthy conditions were maintained throughout the Balason River. Agricultural activities, improper waste disposal, and intense urbanization severely impact these vital reserves. Immediate intervention is absolutely necessary to halt this widespread degradation. Ultimately, policymakers and civic authorities can construct targeted water quality management strategies using these empirical results. The design of vital treatment infrastructure throughout the region can be supported by the scientific foundation presented in this study.

papers.title: Soil Erosion Versus Soil Retention Capacity: An Impact Assessment Of Regulating Ecosystem Service Provision In Iran
papers.summary: The objective of this study was to determine the impact of erosion on soil retention as an ecosystem service and its relationship with soil quality in a mountainous catchment in Iran. In this regard, 42 soil samples were collected from rangelands, rainfed, and irrigated farming areas. Thirteen physical and chemical soil attributes were measured. Principal component analysis was applied to identify a soil quality index (SQI). The respective ranges of soil erosion rates from rangelands, rainfed farming lands, and irrigated farming lands were estimated to be 0.2 – 46.4, 0.18 – 0.20, and 0.00 – 0.18 t ha −1 yr −1 . The SQI estimates ranged between 3.2 – 4.0 for the rangelands compared with corresponding estimates of 4.0 – 5.7 for the rainfed farming lands and 5.7 – 8.4 for the irrigated farming lands. Soil retention was estimated to range between 0 – 0.01 t ha −1 yr −1 (average = 0.005 t ha −1 yr −1 ) for rangelands, 0.01 – 0.03 t ha −1 yr −1 (average = 0.02 t ha −1 yr −1 ) for rainfed farmlands, and 0.03 – 3.5 t ha −1 yr −1 (average = 1.8 t ha −1 yr −1 ) for irrigated farming lands. Negative relationships were observed among soil erosion, soil quality, and soil retention, emphasising the sensitivity of soil quality to the soil erosion rates estimated for different land use types. This study provides evidence for the negative effects of soil erosion under different land uses regarding the degradation of soil quality and soil retention as an ecosystem service.

papers.title: Water and soil loss from purple soil surface under simulated rainfall in Sichuan Basin, Southwest China
papers.source: Journal of Soil Science and Environmental Management
papers.summary: The relationship between rainfall, runoff and soil loss from different slope angles of purple soil still remain unclear despite numerous studies. This study was carried out in the laboratory to estimate runoff and sediment yield from different slope angles (5°, 10°, 15°, 20° and 25°) using Norton rainfall simulator and soil boxes. The soil was subjected to different rainfall intensities of 0.6, 1.1, 1.5 and 1.8 mm/min. Results showed runoff rates decreased in 10° > 20° > 15° > 25° > 5° order with values ranging from 0.26 mm/min for low rainfall intensity (0.6 mm/min) on slope 5° to 1.06 mm/min for simulation experiments with higher rainfall intensity (1.8 mm/min) on slope 10°. Pearson correlation showed a strong correlation (p<0.001) between rainfall intensity and runoff rate. Soil loss linearly increased with runoff rate and slope angles (from 1255.66 gm-2 h-1 under rainfall of 1.8 mm/min on slope 25° to 55.97 gm-2h-1 under 0.6 mm/min on slope 5°). From R² values, runoff strongly explained 53 to 81% variance in the sediment detachment. Assessment of rainfall function on purple soil may help to build conservative measures and strategies in controlling soil loss under different rainfall intensities in Sichuan Basin.

papers.title: GIS-Based Groundwater Recharge and Urbanization Analysis
papers.source: International Journal for Research in Applied Science and Engineering Technology
papers.summary: Groundwater is a vital source of water for domestic, agricultural and industrial use, but rapid urbanization, population growth and over-extraction are placing it under increasing stress. The expansion of built-up areas replaces permeable ground with impervious surfaces, which reduces infiltration and natural recharge while the demand for water continues to rise. This paper presents the framework and preliminary study for a GIS-based assessment of groundwater recharge and the influence of urbanization in selected areas of Manjeri Municipality, Malappuram district, Kerala. Recent studies on GIS–AHP groundwater potential zonation, the effects of urbanization and climate variability on groundwater, the validation of groundwater potential maps and site selection for managed aquifer recharge are reviewed, and an integrated methodology is proposed that combines approximately twenty years of groundwater-level and rainfall data, Google Earth and satellite-based urbanization analysis, GIS thematic layers and statistical modelling in SPSS. The literature review and methodology are complete. Data collection, spatial analysis, modelling and field verification are planned for the next phase, so no conclusions on groundwater conditions are drawn in this paper

papers.title: Stability of Unsaturated Finite Slopes on Critical Slip Surface, an Intelligent Analysis
Extension of the Hydro-Geotechnical TAG-FLOW Model for Urban Flood Analysis: A Preliminary Study in the Chatuchak District, Bangkok, Thailand
Figures
Internal wetting responses of floodplain highway embankments under transient flood boundaries: Cross-scale simulation and service-stage effects
Thermo-hydro coupling characteristics and evolutionary interpretation of the “Crust-Loose-Base” ternary structure in arid earthen sites
papers.summary: Under climate change, surface weathering of arid earthen sites often leads to the formation of a characteristic “Crust-Loose-Base” layered structure, yet its thermo-hydro mechanisms remain unclear. This study investigated the transport properties and pore characteristics of different layers through moisture adsorption–desorption experiments, thermophysical measurements, and microstructural analyses. Results demonstrate that the Loose layer promotes liquid water infiltration and moisture retention, the Base layer facilitates capillary redistribution, while the Crust layer restricts liquid water penetration but allows vapor exchange. Differences in pore architecture, rather than mineral composition, primarily control these transport behaviors. Under thermal gradients, suction variations, and wetting–drying cycles, moisture redistribution may drive water accumulation in the Loose layer and crust formation at the surface. These findings advance the understanding of thermo-hydro coupling mechanisms governing layered structure evolution in arid earthen sites.

papers.title: Application Research of Flexible Facing Layer Soil Nailing Wall Combined with Reinforced Soil Support System in Slope Support Engineering of Meida Expressway
papers.source: SAE technical papers on CD-ROM/SAE technical paper series
papers.summary: For highway embankments in high and steep slope sections, it is often difficult to achieve the designed compaction degree due to the presence of a free face on one side and the lack of lateral confinement during construction, making the slope prone to instability under extreme weather conditions. To address this engineering challenge, this paper proposes a collaborative support system consisting of a flexible-facing soil nailing wall and a reinforced soil structure for the effective stabilization of high and steep slopes. To explain the mechanical behavior and reinforcement mechanism of the system, we established a numerical simulation model via the finite element software PLAXIS 2D, with the in-situ conditions of the unstable high-steep slope section on the eastern extension of Meida Expressway as the numerical prototype. The deformation characteristics and stability evolution of the slope under different surcharge loads at the slope crest and rainfall infiltration conditions were systematically analyzed. The results show that the proposed collaborative support system significantly reduces slope displacement and improves the overall factor of safety of the slope. The anchorage interaction between soil nails and geogrids effectively delays the development and propagation of the plastic zone in the soil mass. Even under extreme surcharge loads at the slope crest or severe rainfall infiltration conditions, the slope still maintains an adequate safety margin. This study reveals the coupled mechanism of mechanical reinforcement and hydraulic regulation in the collaborative support system, providing a theoretical basis and engineering reference for the design of support systems for high and steep slopes under space-limited conditions.

papers.title: Temporal convolutional network-based parameter inversion, deformation forecasting and dual-track early warning for a super- large excavation in water-rich sandy strata
papers.summary: Deformation prediction for super-large excavations in water-rich sandy strata is limited by uncertain soil parameters, while data-driven forecasts alone cannot show whether a deformation trend is abnormal. This study couples the two approaches for the Φ130 m circular excavation of the Shiziyang Bridge west anchorage. Sensitivity analysis of a modified Mohr–Coulomb model showed that the effective friction angle and unloading–reloading reference modulus of the silty clay and fine-sand layers control the deformation. A temporal convolutional network (TCN), trained on 50 Latin hypercube finite-element samples, mapped nine measured responses to these six parameters with a cross-validated mean absolute percentage error (MAPE) of 5.0%, 24% lower than that of the best of five baseline regressors. Calibration reduced the MAPE of the simulated histories from 21.0% to 3.0% for wall displacement and from 29.2% to 5.8% for ground settlement. A second TCN forecast wall displacement 14 days ahead with a MAPE of 4.60%, against 13.09% for persistence. A dual-track rule issues a warning when the two forecasts differ by more than 10% and the forecast exceeds 70% of the 30 mm control value. At nine monitoring points, the rule flagged all three sections with seepage or accelerating deformation, without false alarms.

papers.title: Numerical investigation of wrapped-face back-to-back reinforced soil walls: wall separation and the mobilized earth pressure
papers.summary: Back-to-back reinforced soil walls (RSWs) are widely used for bridge approaches and narrow embankments, but the available numerical evidence derives mostly from rigid or modular facing systems. Unlike rigid facing, a geosynthetic wrap provides negligible flexural rigidity, so lateral earth pressure is resisted only by soil–reinforcement interaction. Plane-strain finite element analyses simulate the staged construction of 6 m high wrapped-face back-to-back RSWs, evaluating wall separation, reinforcement continuity, vertical spacing, foundation stiffness, reinforcement creep and constitutive soil model. The largest change in response occurs when the two reinforced zones lose contact, rather than at the boundary between interacting and independent walls defined in design guidance. Separation increases displacements and tensile loads and lowers the factor of safety. Reinforcement continuity mainly reduces facing deformation, whereas vertical spacing controls both deformation and stability. Softer foundations reduce facing displacement while lowering the factor of safety, so facing displacement alone is an unreliable performance indicator. Over the design life, reinforcement creep increases facing displacement by about 26–30% but relaxes tensile loads. The mobilized earth pressure remains close to the at-rest state with the Hardening Soil model and vertical spacings up to 0.4 m, including after creep, but close to the active state with Mohr–Coulomb.

papers.title: Spatial patterns in indirect effects of human activity on climate, land, and water: comparing top-down and bottom-up clustering approaches
papers.summary: In order to assess the full systemic impact of anthropogenic pressures on climate and land, it is crucial to account for indirect impacts mediated by bio-geophysical processes. These impacts typically display a high spatial heterogeneity. In this study, we systematically compare the ability of top-down and bottom-up clustering approaches to capture the spatial patterns in indirect effects on climate, land, and water. Effect sizes are estimated based on simulations conducted with an offline global spatial vegetation model. Following a top-down approach, we map the resulting global pattern on common natural partitions of the Earth. Cluster validity indices reveal a close alignment between the indirect impacts of land use change on climate and an Earth partition into biomes. In contrast, the indirect impacts of climate- and land use change on surface water runoff are best captured by the Köppen-Geiger climate zones. Adopting a bottom-up approach, we employ multivariate spatially constrained clustering to derive an integrative global partition. Several patches of tropical rainforest on the Indomalayan islands as well as large areas of warm grasslands in Australia are identified as high-impact clusters. The results of this study should be considered illustrative as they are based on only one dynamical vegetation model. Nevertheless, they emphasize the local nature of indirect impacts and elucidate the potential and limitations of both top-down and bottom-up spatial aggregation.

papers.title: Potassium Management under Different Crop Establishment Methods for Improving the Productivity of the Rice (Oryza sativa L.)—Wheat (Triticum aestivum L.) Cropping System: A Review
papers.source: Journal of Global Innovations in Agricultural Sciences
papers.summary: A population of over 150 million in South Asia, particularly in the Indo-Gangetic Plains, relies on the rice-wheat cropping system (RWCS) as the source of their food and means of livelihood. Despite being a necessity of the Green Revolution, problems such as yield stagnation, soil erosion, groundwater depletion, and burning residue pollution are currently straining its long-term sustainability. Traditional practices like puddled transplanted rice followed by conventionally tilled wheat have further strained soil health and increased resource use. Potassium (K), the third most important nutrient after nitrogen and phosphorus, is vital for maintaining crop productivity, yet its use in India remains low. Continuous high crop uptake without adequate replenishment has led to a negative K balance, depleting soil fertility over time. To address this, resource-conserving technologies—such as zero tillage, direct-seeded rice, mechanical transplanting, and crop residue recycling—combined with potassium management can play a key role in restoring soil nutrient pools. Moreover, adopting alternative sources like potassium-solubilizing bacteria and organic amendments (vermicompost, crop residues) can improve potassium availability while reducing dependence on costly imported fertilizers. Integrated potassium management across different crop establishment methods not only improves soil properties but also ensures sustainable productivity and profitability of the RWCS. By embracing these practices, farmers can overcome stagnating yields, preserve soil health, and reduce environmental risks, thereby strengthening the resilience and future of this vital cropping system in South Asia. Keywords: Cropping system, economics, food security, soil health, groundwater, zero tillage, crop residue, insect and pest resistance, potassium management.

papers.title: Ground temperature monitoring in a sandy vadose zone: depth dependence of temperature changes unexplained by heat conduction
papers.summary: Ground temperature varies annually as heat input at the surface propagates by conduction, but rainfall infiltration and other processes can superimpose temperature changes that conduction cannot explain. To determine the depth to which such changes appear, ground temperature was monitored hourly at z = 3, 6, 9 and 12 m for approximately ten months, from October 2025 to July 2026, in a sandy vadose zone with a water table approximately 15 m deep. The annual variation was fitted with a cosine function to remove the conductive annual component, and PELT (Pruned Exact Linear Time), a changepoint detection method, was applied to the residuals. Fourteen changepoints were detected at z = 3 m, whereas only three, two and three changepoints were detected at z = 6, 9 and 12 m, respectively. The temperature changes unexplained by heat conduction therefore concentrate at z = 3 m and diminish markedly at greater depths.

papers.title: Integrating Urban Trees into Flood-Resilient Landscape Design: A Conceptual Framework for Ipoh, Perak, Malaysia
papers.source: Journal of Art Design and Creative Media
papers.summary: Urban flooding creates significant challenges for sustainable urban landscapes, yet urban trees are commonly discussed as hydrological assets rather than integrated elements of flood-resilient landscape design. This conceptual paper proposes a design-oriented framework for examining how urban tree canopy, spatial configuration and surrounding land-use conditions may inform flood-resilient landscape planning in Ipoh, Perak, Malaysia. A focused critical synthesis of nine supplied peer-reviewed studies on urban tree hydrology, stormwater management and landscape configuration was used to identify established mechanisms, contextual constraints and potential planning applications. The literature indicates that rainfall interception, evapotranspiration and root-associated infiltration contribute to stormwater regulation, but their relative effectiveness varies with canopy traits, ground-cover permeability, rainfall conditions and the spatial arrangement of vegetation. The synthesis also identifies an important distinction between demonstrated reductions in runoff and claims about changes in observed flood occurrence. In response, a conceptual landscape design framework is proposed that links vegetation attributes, site conditions, landscape configuration and design interventions to potential stormwater-management functions. The framework prioritizes tree conservation, connected green spaces and context-sensitive planting in combination with appropriate ground-surface and drainage design. The proposed design interpretation emphasizes that neither tree numbers nor canopy percentage alone provides a sufficient basis for flood-resilient intervention. Site suitability, accessible rooting volume, tree–pavement relationships and the continuity of vegetated spaces must also be considered in future design assessment, particularly where urban development creates constraints on permeable surfaces and long-term vegetation management. This contribution reframes urban trees as multifun

papers.title: Hydrogeochemical drivers of salinity intrusion in coastal paddy fields: Soil-water interactions and irrigation implications
papers.summary: Salinity intrusion is a major constraint in coastal paddy agroecosystems, where the dynamic interplay of groundwater, surface water and soil processes determines the quality of irrigation water and crop performance. While previous studies have examined hydrogeochemical processes, soil salinity and crop responses individually, their integration at the field scale remains limited. This review integrates the hydrogeochemical drivers of salinity intrusion, such as seawater mixing, groundwater abstraction, tidal forcing and land-use change and links them explicitly to root-zone salinity dynamics, soil transformations and irrigation suitability. Evidence indicates that salinisation is not a constant process, but rather a spatiotemporally variable phenomenon controlled by groundwater–surface water connectivity, microtopography and in-season hydrological variability under flooded conditions. We argue that root-zone salinity, rather than bulk irrigation water salinity, is the primary determinant of rice stress and productivity in coastal systems. Management strategies such as irrigation–drainage coupling, blended water use, soil amendments and adaptive cropping systems can partially regulate salinity distribution, but single-component interventions often fail under dynamic coastal hydroclimatic conditions. This synthesis highlights the need to reframe salinity intrusion as a coupled hydrogeochemical–soil–crop process and emphasises integrated water–salt balance approaches for sustaining irrigation and productivity in coastal rice agroecosystems.

papers.title: Infraestrutura verde e técnicas compensatórias na mitigação de alagamentos: proposta aplicada à Avenida Marginal Neblina em Araguaína – TO
papers.summary: Accelerated urban growth and soil sealing have caused severe changes in the hydrological cycle of Brazilian cities, resulting in a significant increase in surface runoff volume and the recurrent occurrence of urban flooding events. In this context, this study aims to analyze the operational limitations of conventional urban drainage systems (hygienist approach) and propose the application of rain gardens as a green infrastructure compensatory technique to mitigate flooding on Marginal Neblina Avenue, in Araguaína–TO, Brazil. The methodology adopted is applied, qualitative, descriptive, and exploratory-propositive, based on a specialized literature review, physiographic characterization of the Neblina Creek watershed, local critical event diagnostics, and conceptual interpretation grounded in the principles of the Rational Method and Manning's Equation. The results indicate that the low slope of the avenue, combined with the high impermeability rate of the surrounding area, overloads the underground microdrainage network, rendering it insufficient during intense rainfall events. It is concluded that the decentralized implementation of rain gardens along the median and marginal areas represents a technically viable bioretention solution, effective in dampening peak flows, promoting infiltration, treating diffuse pollution (first flush), and upgrading the urban space.

papers.title: Analysis of The Impact of River Discharge on Embankment Stability and Nature-Based Solutions: A Case Study at The CS-9 Cibingbin Site
papers.summary: River embankments constructed from granular materials excavated during river channel normalization, including gravel, stone, and sand, are particularly susceptible to erosion, seepage, and instability under high-flow conditions. This study examined the effects of river discharge on embankment stability at the CS-9 Cibingbin cross-section in Kuningan Regency, Indonesia, and assessed a hybrid nature-based solution (NBS) incorporating gabion structures and riparian vegetation as a potential stabilization measure. A quantitative numerical case study approach was employed, integrating annual maximum rainfall data from 2018 to 2024, hydraulic simulations using HEC-RAS, and slope stability analyses using GeoStudio SLOPE/W with Bishop's simplified method at station STA 1+875. The results indicated a mean annual maximum rainfall of 139.43 mm and a standard deviation of 35.20 mm, with estimated design flood discharges ranging from 423.2 to 828.0 m³/s along the Cisanggarung–Cijangkelok river reach. The simulated water surface elevation at STA 1+875 increased from 66.84 ft for the two-year return period (Q2) to 67.10 ft for the 25-year return period (Q25). The calculated factor of safety (FoS) decreased substantially from 5.968 under dry conditions to 0.976 under the modeled inundation condition, indicating potential embankment instability. These findings suggested that changes in hydraulic loading and seepage conditions could reduce embankment stability by increasing pore water pressure and decreasing effective shear strength. A hybrid stabilization approach combining permeable gabion structures for toe protection and erosion control with riparian vegetation for potential root reinforcement was recommended as a sustainable mitigation strategy, subject to further geotechnical and hydraulic evaluation.

papers.title: INTEGRATED WATER SUSTAINABILITY INDEX IN THE ALTO LERMA HYDROLOGICAL SUBREGION, MEXICO
papers.summary: Water sustainability is a major challenge in areas where weather variability coincides with intense human pressures. The Alto Lerma Hydrological Subregion in central Mexico presents imbalances resulting from urban growth, agricultural expansion, and aquifer overexploitation. This study develops an Integrated Water Sustainability Index (IWSI) to comparatively evaluate eight basins by integrating five variables: annual precipitation, real evapotranspiration, vegetation cover, irrigated agricultural area, and internal runoff. The information was obtained from official databases, including weather records from the Climate Computing Project (CLICOM) of the National Meteorological Service (SMN), cartographic data from the National Institute of Statistics and Geography (INEGI), and water-related information from the National Water Commission (CONAGUA). The variables were standardized using the min-max method and aggregated with uniform weighting. The results show IWSI values ranging from 0.11 to 0.4, indicating high spatial heterogeneity. Basins with greater vegetation cover and lower agricultural pressure present more favorable conditions, whereas those with high evapotranspiration and intensive irrigation exhibit lower sustainability. Evapotranspiration exceeding 600 mm year-1 and agricultural area exceeding 25 % are associated with low index values. The results confirm that water sustainability depends on the interaction among climate-driven supply, ecological regulation, and productive pressures. The IWSI is a reproducible diagnostic tool that helps identify territorial imbalances and supports differentiated water management at the basin level.

papers.title: A framework for integrated management of flooding and soil erosion using Nature-based Solutions. : An application to the Nyabarongo catchment in Rwanda
papers.summary: Flooding, soil erosion, and sediment transport are interconnected environmental and socio-economic challenges in Rwanda, particularly in the Nyabarongo Catchment, where steep terrain, intense rainfall, land-use change, urbanisation, deforestation, and mining intensify runoff, erosion, and sediment delivery. This thesis investigates how institutional flood risk management, spatial risk assessment, and Naturebased Solutions (NbS) can be integrated to support evidence-based flood and sediment management. Four complementary studies examine institutional flood risk management, flood susceptibility, soil erosion susceptibility, and NbS planning and implementation. The institutional assessment identifies fragmented data management, limited technical capacity, and governance based largely on administrative rather than hydrological boundaries, highlighting the need for proactive catchment-based management. GIS, remote sensing, machine learning, explainable artificial intelligence, and spatial analysis were used to assess flood and erosion susceptibility. Random Forest achieved the highest flood prediction performance (AUC = 0.968; F1-score = 0.92), with 15.6% of the catchment classified as highly to very highly susceptible. For soil erosion, CatBoost achieved an AUC of 0.974 and F1-score of 0.91, with approximately half of the catchment classified as moderately to very highly susceptible. Stakeholder and documentary evidence indicate widespread implementation and perceived benefits of NbS, but limited monitoring, technical and financial constraints, fragmented coordination, and maintenance challenges hinder evaluation of their long-term effectiveness. The thesis proposes an integrated framework linking spatial assessment, site-specific NbS selection, field validation, continuous monitoring, stakeholder participation, adaptive governance, and evidence-based scaling, offering transferable insights for other data-constrained tropical catchments.

papers.title: Experimental Study on Crumb Rubber Modified Porous Asphalt Pavement for Enhancing Groundwater Recharge
papers.source: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
authors: Prajakta Amar Pattanshetti, J. A. Patil
papers.summary: The increasing development of impervious urban surfaces has contributed to higher stormwater runoff and reduced natural groundwater recharge. Porous asphalt pavement provides an effective alternative by allowing rainfall to infiltrate through interconnected air voids. The present study experimentally investigates the use of crumb rubber in porous asphalt pavement to improve its engineering performance while promoting waste tyre utilization. Crumb rubber is incorporated at different contents, and the effect of modification is evaluated through basic bitumen properties including penetration, softening point, and ductility. Porous asphalt mixtures are further assessed for Indirect Tensile Strength (ITS) and permeability to determine the combined mechanical and hydraulic performance. The experimental results are compared to identify the crumb rubber content providing a suitable balance between pavement strength and water infiltration capacity. The study also considers the potential of porous asphalt for enhancing groundwater recharge and reducing surface runoff. A cost–benefit analysis is included to evaluate the economic feasibility of incorporating waste crumb rubber in porous asphalt pavement. The study aims to establish a practical and sustainable pavement solution that combines improved performance, groundwater recharge, waste tyre utilization, and economic benefits.

papers.title: Rainfall redistribution and water use patterns of four planted forest types in a small watershed in the exposed pisha sandstone region of the loess plateau
papers.summary: Water availability is a key limiting factor for vegetation restoration and ecosystem stability in the Pisha sandstone region of the Loess Plateau. However, quantitative evidence on how different planted species partition rainfall, modify soil infiltration, and differentiate their vertical water-uptake niches under water-limited conditions remains scarce for this lithologically unique region. This study addressed three questions: (i) how the four species partition rainfall into interception, throughfall and stemflow; (ii) how they modify soil infiltration; and (iii) how their water sources shift vertically across the growing season, and what this implies for species selection in vegetation restoration. Four dominant planted species ( Caragana korshinskii , Hippophae rhamnoides , Pinus tabuliformis , and Prunus sibirica ) were investigated in a representative small watershed, with three replicate plots established for each species. Field observations included canopy rainfall redistribution, double-ring infiltration experiments, continuous soil moisture monitoring across the 0–60 cm soil profile, sap flow measurements, and hydrogen and oxygen isotope tracing of soil and xylem water during the growing season. The MixSIAR Bayesian mixing model was applied to quantify seasonal variations in plant water sources, and linear mixed-effects models were used to evaluate interspecific differences. The results showed that H. rhamnoides and C. korshinskii exhibited strong canopy interception capacity (averaging 76.5% and 59.4%, respectively), whereas P. sibirica produced the highest stemflow volume. C. korshinskii showed the highest initial (9.80 mm min − ¹), steady-state (4.42 mm min − ¹) and average (5.70 mm min − ¹) infiltration rates, while H. rhamnoides showed the lowest infiltration capacity (steady-state rate of 1.05 mm min − ¹). All species displayed distinct diurnal sap flow patterns, reflecting different water regulation strategies. Isotope analysis revealed clear season

papers.title: XDA28010202 Principles and Key Technologies for Erosion Resistance Enhancement and Runoff Regulation of Black Soil on Sloping Farmland: Dataset on Runoff Regulation and Erosion Control via Erosion-Resistant and Water-Retaining Materials
papers.summary: This dataset consists of long-term positioned monitoring data obtained from field monitoring plots of erosion-resistant and water-retaining material technology in the Hailun demonstration area from 2022 to 2025. It is primarily used to evaluate the regulatory effects of erosion-resistant and water-retaining material technology on soil structure, soil water infiltration, rainfall runoff, sediment loss, and crop production in sloping cropland. The dataset covers soil background physicochemical properties, soil pore characteristics, soil aggregate composition, rainfall runoff and sediment loss, as well as crop yield and biomass in the erosion-resistant and water-retaining material monitoring plots.

papers.title: Causal-stage attribution for debris-flow cascades in changing mountain regions: illustrated by the 2022 Bicharh Nallah debris flow
papers.summary: Debris-flow inventories usually record where and when events occur but often compress source initiation, transformation and runout into one whole-event label. This is problematic in high mountains, where rainfall, melt, ground-ice thaw, rock–ice failure, lake release and channel entrainment can occupy different causal roles within a single cascade. We propose an evidence-graded six-stage attribution architecture that records conditioning context, dynamic preconditioning, proximate initiator, release mechanism, transformation and routing/runout separately. Water source and external forcing are treated as attributes rather than stages, and each stage retains its evidence basis, corroboration, plausible alternatives and unresolved status. The framework is designed to reduce prediction-time data leakage, align monitoring signals with the decisions they can support, and distinguish background climate influence from event-scale initiation. The 2022 Bicharh Nallah debris flow in northern Pakistan shows this framework, with rainfall identified as the immediate trigger, snowmelt as an additional water source, and subsequent boulder blockage controlling downstream flow. We outline benchmark inventories and prospective tests against binary baselines to determine when stage-resolved attribution improves interpretability, transferability, and forecast updating.

papers.title: LITERATURE REVIEW ON MODIFIED DOTCON-BASED PERMEABLE PAVEMENT SYSTEM FOR URBAN FLOOD MITIGATION AND RAINWATER HARVESTING
papers.summary: Rapid urbanisation and the increase in impervious surfaces have affected the natural movement of rainwater, contributing to surface runoff, water accumulation and urban flooding.Permeable pavement systems have been studied as an alternative to conventional impermeable pavement because they allow rainwater to pass through the pavement structure and enter the underlying layers.Pervious concrete and permeable pavement systems also provide opportunities for stormwater management, groundwater recharge and rainwater harvesting.The literature reviewed in this paper covers the hydrological performance of permeable pavements, mechanical properties of pervious concrete, pavement design under traffic loading, rainwater harvesting systems and water-quality performance.The reviewed studies indicate that pavement performance depends on the properties of the surface layer, aggregate base and sub-base, underlying soil, and the provision of suitable drainage and storage arrangements.The literature also identifies the importance of balancing permeability and structural strength and considering clogging and maintenance during pavement design.The present project proposes a modification of the DOTCON-based permeable pavement concept by incorporating an additional rainwater collection, filtration and storage arrangement.The proposed modification aims to collect a portion of the water passing through the pavement and make it available for potential non-potable reuse while retaining the stormwatermanagement function of the pavement.This review provides the technical background and identifies the research requirements for evaluating the proposed system.

papers.title: How does intercropping perennial grains with alfalfa impact soil physical and hydraulic properties?
papers.summary: Perennial cereal–legume intercropping systems are promoted as climate-smart and resilient alternatives to annual monocultures; however, their effects on soil physical and hydraulic properties remain poorly quantified, particularly for developed perennial cereals; ACE1 perennial rye ( Secale cereale L.) and intermediate wheatgrass (IWG) ( Thinopyrum intermedium ). This study evaluated how intercropping these perennial cereal grain crops (PCGCs) with alfalfa ( Medicago sativa L. ) influences soil physical structure and hydraulic functioning across five field locations in Alberta, Canada. Sites were established in spring 2022, and soils were sampled in summer 2024. Using a split–split plot design, we assessed crop utilization (forage or grain), seeding arrangement, and crop treatment (intercrop or monocrop) effects on soil physical and hydraulic properties at 10–15 and 30–35 cm depths. Topsoil organic carbon (SOC) stock was also measured at 0–15 cm depth increment. Intercropping enhanced soil hydraulic properties in a site-specific manner. Compared to monocultures, PCGC–alfalfa intercrops increased field capacity (FC), plant-available water capacity (PAWC), and meso and microporosity by 6–45 %, with stronger effects at 30–35 cm depth. Unsaturated hydraulic conductivity varied among sites, but IWG-based intercrops exhibited 20–40 % higher values than ACE1 under comparable management. SOC–hydraulic relationships were context dependent; intercrops strengthened SOC water retention linkages, particularly at high-carbon sites. Multivariate analyses associated intercrops with improved water retention, pore connectivity, and S-index, whereas monocrops aligned with increased bulk density and reduced hydraulic function. Overall, intercropping PCGCs with alfalfa improved soil hydraulic functioning, primarily through enhanced water dynamics rather than major structural change, highlighting their potential to increase soil resilience across diverse environments.

papers.title: XDA28010202 Principles and Key Technologies for Erosion Resistance Enhancement and Runoff Regulation of Black Soil on Sloping Farmland: Dataset on Runoff Regulation and Erosion Control via Rapid Infiltration Zone Technology
papers.summary: This dataset consists of long-term positioned monitoring data obtained from field monitoring plots of rapid infiltration zone technology in the Hailun demonstration area from 2022 to 2025. It is primarily used to evaluate the regulatory effects of rapid infiltration zone technology on soil structure, soil water infiltration, rainfall runoff, sediment loss, and crop production in sloping cropland.The dataset covers soil background physicochemical properties, soil pore characteristics, soil aggregate composition, soil saturated hydraulic conductivity, in situ infiltration characteristics, rainfall runoff and sediment loss, as well as crop yield and biomass in the rapid infiltration zone monitoring plots.

papers.title: Maintenance Priorities for Permeable Structures and Conventional Stormwater Drainage in Ilala, Tanzania
papers.summary: Stormwater maintenance must address both the infiltration function of permeable structures and the conveyance function of conventional drainage. This study identifies maintenance concerns in Ilala, Dar es Salaam, and develops a condition-based framework for managing the two asset groups together. A descriptive reanalysis used tabulated aggregate questionnaire counts from 52 drainage personnel and service providers, along with 10 archival records of rainfall and outlet volumes. Fifty-five questionnaires were distributed, 53 were returned, and 52 were retained. Six technical domains were examined. Means and sample standard deviations were recalculated from the response counts, and indicator direction was checked against the questionnaire anchors before constructing relative severity indices. Inlet or matrix clogging had the highest severity index in both asset groups, at 0.846. Conduit blockage or loss of subsurface storage followed, at 0.819 for conventional drainage and 0.815 for permeable structures. Treatment effectiveness received favourable ratings, whereas retention and attenuation ratings indicated a need for further performance investigation. Vegetation required separate interpretation because channel obstruction and the vitality of designed planting were scored in opposite directions. Across the archival records, the aggregate fraction of rainfall volume absent from the recorded outlet was 60.1% for permeable structures and 23.1% for conventional drainage. These figures describe incomplete water balances and do not establish treatment effects or validate a predictive model. The proposed framework links inspection, sediment control, maintenance, and verification while retaining structural safety and storm-capacity checks. The findings support coordinated maintenance of infiltration and conveyance, with field measurements needed to establish hydraulic benefits, determine appropriate intervention thresholds, and assess performance changes after maintenance.

papers.title: Study on the rising trend of groundwater levels in Beijing and its impact on underground space
papers.summary: Most large and medium-sized cities in China are water-deficient. Long-term overexploitation of groundwater has led to the deterioration of the urban geo-environment, whereas recent measures such as ecological water replenishment and groundwater abstraction control have substantially alleviated this trend. However, groundwater level rise may also cause damage to underground space and affect the development and utilization of underground space resources. Taking the Beijing Plain as an example, this study investigates the trend and patterns of urban groundwater level rise from 2019 to 2025, as well as its impact on the development and utilization of underground space. On this basis, groundwater regulation countermeasures are examined using the marginal analysis method from environmental economics. The results show that ecological water replenishment in Beijing has raised the average groundwater level in the urban plain area by 14.81 m compared with that in 2015. Groundwater level rise exerts multiple damage effects on existing underground space structures, including structural corrosion and deterioration, leakage, anti-uplift failure, increased foundation settlement, and differential hydrostatic pressure-induced damage. It also increases groundwater-related disaster risks during the construction of underground engineering projects and increases the costs of construction dewatering and groundwater cutoff measures. Through a comprehensive benefit analysis of groundwater level rise, this study proposes a multi-level prevention and control framework comprising "dynamic regulation of rising groundwater levels, improvement of anti-uplift design standards, enhancement of underground space resilience, optimization of groundwater control technologies for underground engineering, and establishment of a groundwater level monitoring and early-warning mechanism." papers.title: Enhancing soil stability and mitigating splash erosion through cyanobacterial inoculation under two contrasting soil salinity–slope settings
papers.summary: Introduction Soil erosion threatens land resources, yet splash erosion, its initial stage, remains insufficiently studied. Objectives This study evaluates the effects of cyanobacterial inoculation on splash erosion and soil stability under two salinity–slope settings: lower salinity at a 10% slope and higher salinity at a 5% slope. Methods Triplicate experimental plots were established using soils from two salinity–slope settings and randomly assigned to cyanobacterial inoculation or untreated control treatments. We uniformly applied cultivated, extracted, and propagated cyanobacteria to the soil surface, then incubated the plots for 60 days under controlled conditions. Splash erosion was subsequently simulated using a rainfall simulator under specified intensity and duration, with splash gutters installed on both sides of each plot to collect eroded soil. Soil loss was quantified, and soil stability was evaluated before rainfall simulation. Results Cyanobacterial inoculation reduced mean total splash erosion in both settings, from 1.693 to 0.565 g/m 2 under lower salinity and 10% slope, and from 0.727 to 0.329 g/m 2 under higher salinity and 5% slope. Welch's t tests indicated statistically significant treatment differences ( p = 0.0441 and p = 0.0025, respectively). Mean soil‐stability indices also increased following inoculation, from 1.573 to 7.374 and from 2.006 to 6.929, respectively; however, these differences did not reach statistical significance ( p = 0.0516 and p = 0.0703). Conclusions Cyanobacterial inoculation consistently reduced splash erosion across salinity–slope settings, showing promise as a bio‐based soil stabilizer. Larger experiments are needed to confirm these effects and support reliable restoration.

papers.title: Jessour: A traditional and resilient strategy for improving water security and restoring degraded drylands
papers.source: MELSpace (ICARDA (The International Center for Agricultural Research in Dry Areas))
papers.summary: This brief highlights the importance of Jessour, a traditional water-harvesting and soil conservation system widely used in southern Tunisia and other arid and semi-arid regions of North Africa. Constructed using earthen or stone embankments across shallow valleys and wadis, Jessour capture surface runoff, improve water infiltration, retain soil moisture, and trap fertile sediments, enabling agricultural production under conditions of scarce and irregular rainfall. The brief describes the main structural components of Jessour, including the dike (tabia), terrace (jessr), and catchment area (impluvium), and explains their combined role in reducing soil erosion, regulating water flow, and supporting ecosystem functions. By integrating trees, annual crops, forage resources, and livestock, Jessour sustain diversified agroecological systems that enhance agrobiodiversity, strengthen food security, and support rural livelihoods. Despite their environmental and socioeconomic benefits, many Jessour systems face degradation and abandonment due to land fragmentation, demographic changes, climate extremes, and the loss of traditional knowledge. Revitalizing these systems requires rehabilitation, regular structural maintenance, improved water management, community participation, and supportive public policies. Combining indigenous knowledge with appropriate engineering solutions can strengthen climate resilience, restore degraded drylands, improve water security, and promote sustainable agricultural production in vulnerable landscapes.

papers.title: Synergistic effects of multiple factors on surface runoff initiation time at mountainous hillslopes: A case study in the upper reach of the Danjiangkou Reservoir, China
papers.summary: Study region The Guanshan River watershed, China. Study focus Predicting surface runoff initiation time ( T sur ) is critical for flash flood early warning in mountainous watersheds. We quantified how rainfall intensity ( RI ), slope gradient ( S ), soil thickness distribution pattern ( STDP ), and initial soil moisture ( θ ini ) jointly regulate T sur through 72 laboratory simulations and 26 field plots. Three-way ANOVA decomposed the main and interaction effects, and two threshold models derived from the fitted T sur model ( CR and CR + ASM ) were validated on independent field plots. New hydrological insights for the region T sur decreased with RI and θ ini , each following a power function. The accelerating effect of S depended on RI : raising S from 5° to 15° and 25° shortened T sur by 60.5% and 75.1% at 30 mm/h but only 33.0%–66.0% at 120 mm/h, reflecting a shift from lateral-drainage to infiltration excess. RI × S and the STDP -involving interactions explained 19.19%–20.07% and 30.96%–34.87% of T sur variance, showing STDP acts as a pathway regulator, not a direct control. The fitted T sur model yielded cumulative rainfall ( CR ) thresholds CR 1 – CR 4 that partition runoff generation into three stages; which differed between thick and thin soil layers ( CR 4 = 38.64 vs. 32.67 mm) because CR alone ignores the initial storage deficit. Reformulating this criterion as CR + ASM ≥ W crit nearly eliminated this difference (≤2.32 mm) and reproduced runoff initiation under extremely dry conditions where rainfall-only indicators failed.

papers.title: Information-theoretic modeling of landslide susceptibility using mostly categorical spatial data
papers.summary: Landslide susceptibility mapping with machine learning should make full use of inherently informative categorical layers such as lithology, soil type, and land use, yet these variables usually enter models in a diminished, encoded form. Reconstructability Analysis (RA), an information-theoretic method based on Shannon entropy, uses categorical data directly and produces transparent, interpretable models. We applied RA to two contiguous Oregon Coast Range (USA) watersheds (3,500 km²) rated Very High Risk for landslides by the Federal Emergency Management Agency, using ~9,000 landslide deposits mapped mostly from LiDAR by the Oregon Department of Geology and Mineral Industries (DOGAMI), with DOGAMI lithology, Soil Survey, and National Land Cover Database layers; terrain variables were discretized into optimized bins. Variable importance analysis led to stratification into volcanic and sedimentary lithologies, with landslide rates of 44 % and 60 %. The best RA models reached 75 % (volcanic) and 71 % (sedimentary) test accuracy, nearly as good as Random Forest, while remaining interpretable in terms of named soil, landform, and rock units. Their probability tables give landslide likelihood for specific combinations of landform, geology, and elevation; in the sedimentary stratum, two andic soil subgroups emerged as most landslide-prone, consistent with high water retention. The tables are provided as a supplement.

papers.title: Rainfall-Runoff Simulation and Hydrological Response Assessment using SWAT Model in an Urban Watershed
papers.summary: Rapid urbanization and climate variability have substantially altered the hydrological response of urban watersheds, resulting in increased surface runoff, reduced infiltration, and a higher frequency of urban flooding. Understanding these changes is essential for sustainable watershed management and flood risk mitigation. This study evaluates the rainfall-runoff response of the Wakad urban watershed in the Mula River Basin, Pune, India, using the soil and water assessment tool (SWAT) implemented through the QSWAT interface. A high-resolution modelling framework was developed using a 30 m digital elevation model (DEM), 10 m land use/land cover (LULC) data, FAO soil data, and daily hydro-meteorological data obtained from NASA POWER for the period 1995-2023. The watershed was delineated into 28 sub-basins and corresponding hydrological response units (HRUs) to represent the spatial variability of terrain, land use, and soil characteristics. Model calibration and validation were performed using SWAT-CUP with the SUFI-2 algorithm. The calibrated model showed satisfactory performance, with a Nash-Sutcliffe Efficiency (NSE) of 0.72 and a coefficient of determination (R²) of 0.78, indicating reliable simulation of streamflow. The simulation results revealed that increasing urbanization and expansion of impervious surfaces significantly increased surface runoff and reduced infiltration within the watershed. Peak runoff occurred during high-intensity monsoon events, with substantial temporal and spatial variability among sub-basins. The spatial distribution of runoff identified highly urbanized areas as being more susceptible to elevated runoff generation compared with relatively vegetated areas. The findings demonstrate the capability of the SWAT model to quantify long-term hydrological responses to land-use change in a rapidly urbanizing watershed. papers.title: A preliminary study of runoff-generated waste dump debris flow in the mountain cryosphere
papers.summary: Waste dump debris flows pose significant risks as man-made disasters. The development of large-scale infrastructure in the Tibetan Plateau of China has led to the accumulation of tunnel waste in the mountain cryosphere. To investigate the erosion process and initiation mechanism of waste dump debris flows caused by concentrated runoff in the mountain cryosphere, we examined the erosion characteristics of the Duoxiongla waste dump near Mount Namcha Barwa. Subsequently, we performed flume experiments using various waste dump geometries, considering the geomorphic and hydrological characteristics of the Longjiaqu catchment. The results reveal that the waste dump in the mountain cryosphere undergoes significant rill and lateral erosion caused by snowmelt runoff, which is further exacerbated by rainfall. Initially, the waste dump experiences headward erosion and gully erosion when subjected to simulated concentrated runoff. As the water discharge increases, the erosion gully widens and deepens, forming an erosion channel. With intensified surface runoff, the erosion channel transforms into a channelized debris flow, causing significant erosion of the channel bed. The water discharge required to trigger channelized debris flow increases with steeper slopes, assuming similar waste dump volumes. Channelized debris flow can occur when snowmelt and rainfall coincide, especially in cases of inadequate design. Hydromechanical analysis reveals that waste dump debris flow occurs as water discharge increases due to the drag force on the surface of the waste dump, seepage force inside the waste dump, and gradual saturation or near saturation of the shallow portion.

papers.title: IMPACTS OF CONTEMPORARY GLOBAL CHANGES ON THE WATER CYCLE OF THE BRESTNITSA KARST GEOSYSTEM IN NORTHERN BULGARIA
papers.summary: Brestnitsa Karst Geosystem (BKG) was formed in the Pre-Balkans in Northern Bulgaria.It is developed in Mesozoic organogenic limestones with a very high carbonate content.A complete karst morphological complex has been formed in the relief of the geosystem, which is the result of the combination of autogenous and allogenic types of karst.The BKG region is located in the transitional area between the subtropical and temperate climate.The karst aquifer is recharged by infiltration through the aeration zone of precipitation, irrigation and waste household and fecal waters from livestock farms and inflow of river waters and periodic surface runoff of precipitation waters into sinkholes.The specific structure of the karst geosystem is the reason why its water cycle is very sensitive to global changes of both natural and anthropogenic types and is highly vulnerable to pollution (mechanical, chemical, bacteriological).This is a serious problem, because the geosystem drains into the karst spring Glava Panega, which is the highest flow concentrated spring in Bulgaria.Its waters are used for industrial and drinking-domestic water supply.The aim of this study is to track and analyze the consequences of global changes on the water cycle through application of a geosystem approach and the original model for integrated monitoring of karst geosystems (MIKS).Special attention is paid to the sources of anthropogenic pressure influenced by socio-economic changes in regional, national and global aspects and their impact on the pollution of karst waters.

papers.title: Linking a RUSLE-derived erosion proxy to clustered shallow landslides triggered by extreme rainfall: evidence from Typhoon Doksuri in Laishui County, Northern China
papers.summary: Extreme rainfall can trigger widespread shallow landsliding, yet accumulated rainfall alone does not adequately explain its spatial concentration. We examined 15,622 landslides mapped following Typhoon Doksuri in Laishui County, northern China, of which 15,387 were retained for modelling. A RUSLE-derived event erosion proxy (EEP) was constructed by combining 10-day accumulated rainfall, soil erodibility, slope length and steepness, and land-cover factors. Its log-transformed form, EEP′ = ln (EEP + 1), showed a clearer positive association with landslide number density and area percentage than accumulated rainfall alone. Among four logistic regression models, the model incorporating both rainfall and EEP′ alongside conventional conditioning factors achieved the best discrimination and fit (five-fold AUC = 0.7736; AIC = 33,938.81). Spatial-block validation yielded the same model ranking, with the combined model achieving the highest AUC (0.7489). Component-wise comparisons indicated additional improvement in model fit, while random forest analysis identified EEP′ as an influential predictor. These findings support the use of EEP′ as a readily derived, interpretable indicator for characterising spatial differences in shallow-landslide occurrence and supporting regional screening after extreme rainfall. Its broader applicability remains to be tested across other events and regions.

papers.title: Analysis the Characteristics and Performance of Polyethersulfone-Carbon Nanotube Membranes Fabricated Using Electric Field Method for Water Filtration Applications
papers.summary: This study aims to address the effect of Carbon Nanotube (CNT) addition on the characteristics and performance of polyethersulfone (PES) membranes fabricated using the Electric Field method. Four PES membranes were fabricated with addition of CNT and denoted as SM0 (0% CNT), SM1 (0.5% CNT), SM2 (1% CNT), and SM3 (1.5% CNT). SEM observations showed average pore sizes of 0.62±0.12 μm to 0.82±0.18 μm, and AFM images showed the ability of CNTs to increase topographical complexity. The tensile test results indicated that addition of CNT increased the tensile strength of the membrane. The TGA and DTG test graphs showed that addition of CNT can increase the thermal resistance of the membrane. FTIR spectra were in agreement with characteristic PES functional groups. The XRD data showed that the amorphous nature remains dominant, indicating that this composite membrane successfully combines the mechanical strength and functional properties of CNTs without sacrificing the intrinsic pore structure of the PES polymer. Addition of CNT to the membrane increased its hydrophilicity, as evidenced by decrease in water contact angle on the membrane. Addition of CNT can also increase the membrane permeability, as indicated by an increase in the membrane permeability values in the range of 1 to 6 bar. In terms of durability, adding CNT to the membrane can increase its durability, meaning that membranes with added CNT can last longer than pure PES membranes.

Experimental and numerical analysis of damage, stability, and seepage in underground anti-scour walls
papers.summary: To investigate the damage evolution and seepage control performance of underground anti-scour walls under complex hydraulic environments, concrete damage tests were conducted to elucidate the damage deterioration process. Subsequently, a numerical model of the anti-scour wall construction was established to analyze its structural stability and anti-seepage effectiveness under varying degrees of concrete damage and different water levels. The results indicate that the presence of prefabricated cracks reduces the peak strength of the specimens by 40% to 70% compared to intact specimens, and the degree of deterioration exhibits anisotropy. The established damage constitutive model effectively describes the complete stress-strain process of fissured concrete. Numerical simulations reveal that the anti-scour wall effectively blocks the horizontal seepage path of groundwater, forcing water to flow around it. This creates a hydraulic head difference between the inner and outer sides of the wall, demonstrating its excellent seepage control capability. Further analysis shows that even under extreme conditions involving elevated flood levels and wall damage, the H-shaped anti-scour wall effectively inhibits pore pressure transmission without experiencing seepage instability, proving its substantial structural safety redundancy.

Nonclassical Turing instabilities induced by superdiffusive transport in FitzHugh-Nagumo dynamics
papers.summary: We investigate diffusion-driven instabilities in a modified FitzHugh–Nagumo-type activator–inhibitor system with superdiffusive transport modeled by fractional Laplacian operators with different diffusion orders for the activator and the inhibitor. A linear stability analysis yields explicit expressions for the instability threshold and the critical wavenumber and shows that superdiffusion modifies the band of unstable modes and the characteristic spatial scale of emerging patterns. We show that the threshold depends only on the ratio of the fractional exponents, on the kinetic parameters and on the reaction–transport parameter Γ , while it is independent of the individual diffusion orders once their ratio is fixed. The spatial scale is controlled by the diffusion orders and the domain size. When the two species have different fractional diffusion orders, their relative transport strength becomes wavelength-dependent. In particular, when the inhibitor has the higher fractional diffusion order, stationary instabilities may arise even when the scaled inhibitor-to-activator transport parameter is below unity, a regime excluded by the classical activator–inhibitor Turing criterion. A weakly nonlinear analysis near threshold provides the amplitude equation governing nonlinear saturation and reveals that superdiffusion promotes subcritical behavior. We also analyze the interaction between stationary and oscillatory instabilities near Turing–Hopf codimension-two points. All analytical results are supported by numerical simulations.

Prioritizing Fuel Treatments to Reduce Post-Fire Debris Flow Risk in Utah
papers.summary: Wildfire is a natural part of many forest ecosystems, but in the western United States, wildfires have become larger, more frequent, and more severe in recent decades. There are serious problems after severe wildfire, including erosion, flooding, and debris flows that threaten water quality, roads, and communities. Because of this, land managers need better ways to decide where fuel treatments, such as prescribed burning or thinning, can most effectively reduce wildfire damage and post-fire risks. In this dissertation, I studied how fuel treatments might reduce wildfire severity and lower the risk of post-fire debris flows in Utah. First, I built a model to predict how severely forests are likely to burn across the state. Next, I used simulated treatment scenarios to test how different fuel treatments changed wildfire severity in different forest types and under different weather conditions. Finally, I applied those results to real watersheds in Utah to estimate how treatments could reduce post-fire debris-flow risk. The results showed that treatment effectiveness depends strongly on forest type. In some forests, especially ponderosa pine, spruce-fir, and lodgepole pine, reducing fuels had a strong effect on lowering fire severity. In other forest types, weather played a larger role, which made treatments less effective. Across most forests, treatments that reduced both canopy fuels and surface fuels produced the greatest reductions in wildfire severity. At the watershed scale, treatment costs and benefits also varied. Prescribed burning was generally the most cost-effective treatment. In several watersheds, including Electric Lake, Big Cottonwood Canyon, Panguitch Lake, and Rockport, cost-effective treatments provided the greatest reduction in post-fire risk for the money invested, making them especially important areas for management. papers.title: Insights into the February 2026 Floods in the Tropical Andes of Southern Peru from Satellites and Models
papers.summary: Flash floods triggered by intense rainfall during El Niño Costero events pose a major hazard in the Tropical Andes of southern Peru. In February 2026, two consecutive extreme rainfall events caused catastrophic flooding and debris flows in Arequipa, resulting in loss of life, widespread infrastructure damage, and major disruptions to essential services. This study investigates the meteorological conditions associated with these flood-producing storms and evaluates the performance of near-real-time (NRT) and standard versions of the IMERG, GSMaP, and PERSIANN satellite precipitation products in capturing their spatial and temporal evolution. ERA5 reanalysis indicates that enhanced low-level Pacific moisture transport interacting with the steep western slopes of the Andes created favorable conditions for localized afternoon convection and intense rainfall over the Arequipa region. Rain gauge observations revealed highly localized hourly rainfall exceeding 20 mm h-1 during the two flood events. Among the satellite products evaluated, IMERG most accurately reproduced the spatial distribution and total accumulation of precipitation, including the localized rainfall maximum over Arequipa, whereas GSMaP and PERSIANN substantially underestimated rainfall amounts. Although the NRT products generally captured the timing and spatial organization of the rainfall better than their standard counterparts, all products underestimated peak rainfall intensity during the most intense convective periods. These findings demonstrate the value of satellite precipitation products for situational awareness and flood monitoring in mountainous regions with sparse ground observations while highlighting the continuing challenges of accurately representing short-duration, terrain-induced extreme rainfall in operational precipitation estimates.

papers.summary: Daerah Dermaji, Kabupaten Banyumas, Jawa Tengah, merupakan bagian dari Cekungan Banyumas yang merekam perkembangan geologi berupa sedimentasi laut dalam, aktivitas vulkanisme, deformasi tektonik, dan proses geomorfik. Penelitian ini bertujuan merekonstruksi sejarah geologi Daerah Dermaji berdasarkan analisis stratigrafi, karakteristik litologi, hubungan antar satuan batuan, struktur geologi, dan lingkungan pengendapan. Metode yang digunakan berupa analisis stratigrafi yang mencakup rangkaian integrasi dari observasi lapangan, analisis petrografi dan mikropaleontologi. Hasil penelitian menunjukkan bahwa stratigrafi daerah penelitian dari tua ke muda tersusun atas Formasi Kumbang (Tmpk), Formasi Halang (Tmph), dan Formasi Tapak (Tpt). Formasi Kumbang berumur Miosen Tengah hingga Miosen Akhir tersusun atas breksi vulkanik berfragmen andesit yang diendapkan melalui debris flow pada bagian upper fan sistem submarine fan. Formasi Halang berumur Miosen Akhir hingga Pliosen Awal tersusun atas batupasir gampingan, batupasir tufan, perselingan batupasir–batulempung, dan breksi vulkanik yang diendapkan melalui arus turbidit pada zona middle fan hingga upper fan. Formasi ini memiliki hubungan menjari dengan Formasi Kumbang dan menunjukkan lingkungan batimetri Batial Atas hingga Batial Bawah. Formasi Tapak berumur Pliosen Awal hingga Pliosen Tengah terendapkan selaras di atas Formasi Halang pada lingkungan laut dalam dengan batimetri Batial Atas. Deformasi kompresional pada Pliosen–Pleistosen membentuk Sinklin Dermaji dan Sesar Turun Gumelar, kemudian diikuti pelapukan, erosi, dan denudasi berkembang hingga membentuk kondisi geomorfologi daerah penelitian saat ini.

papers.title: Predicting soil-water characteristic curve evolution using pore-scale modelling approach
papers.source: Journal of Natural and Agricultural Sciences
papers.summary: Soils in construction are difficult to predict due to their deformability and complex composition. In unsaturated states, suction from air–water interfaces controls hydro-mechanical behavior by influencing interparticle forces. Environmental changes modify suction and cause shrinkage or expansion. The soil-water characteristic curve links suction and saturation, improving constitutive models and enabling better prediction of soil response under varying conditions.

papers.summary: Infrastructure earthworks require soils with adequate strength, manageable deformation and suitable hydraulic behaviour. Conventional stabilisation with cement and lime can achieve these requirements, but their manufacture has substantial negative environmental effects. Biopolymers offer a potential means of reducing reliance on conventional binders, but their performance is often assessed through strength tests under partially saturated conditions. Their behaviour in saturated and/or near-saturated conditions, effects on compressibility and drainage, and the benefits of combining them with a traditional stabiliser like hydrated lime remain insufficiently understood. This study addresses these gaps to establish when biopolymer-hydrated lime treatment can provide useful soil improvement. An experimental programme investigated London clay, Ligurian sandy silt, pyroclastic silty sand and Karlsruhe fine sand. Treatment of these soils with Guar gum (GG), xanthan gum (XG) and agar gum (AG) was examined either alone or as partial replacements for hydrated lime (HL), at a fixed total stabiliser content of 3% of dry soil mass. Atterberg limits and standard Proctor tests characterised London clay consistency and compaction; oedometer, evaporation and direct shear tests examined the hydromechanical responses of the coarser soils. Saturated consolidated drained triaxial tests further assessed untreated, HL-treated and AG-containing Karlsruhe fine sand under effective confining stresses of 100, 300 and 600 kPa. HL and GG had only a marginal effect on standard Proctor compaction characteristics. papers.title: Assessment and mapping of soil moisture at field capacity using machine learning methods in the Central Chernozem Belt of Russia
papers.summary: Soil moisture at field capacity (SM FC ) is a key soil hydraulic property for assessing water-storage capacity, irrigation requirements, and crop-water availability, yet its regional distribution is difficult to characterize because it is controlled by interacting soil, climatic, topographic, and land-surface factors. To address the logistical constraints of direct regional matric potential measurements, this study applied an indirect, pedotransfer function (PTF)-augmented digital soil mapping framework to estimate and map SM FC at 0–30 cm depth and a matric potential of − 33 kPa across the Central Chernozem Belt of Russia using an explainable machine learning framework. A total of 2157 geo-referenced soil samples collected between 2023 and 2025 were combined with remote-sensing, terrain, climatic, geological, and spatial covariates defined within the SCORPAN framework. SM FC was estimated from van Genuchten water-retention parameters derived using pedotransfer functions, and three machine-learning algorithms, namely artificial neural network (ANN), support vector machine (SVM), and random forest (RF), were trained and independently evaluated using a 70:30 calibrations–validation design. The RF model provided the most accurate predictions in both datasets, achieving R 2 = 0.81, RMSE = 1.93, and PRD = 3.17 during calibration and R 2 = 0.89, RMSE = 1.45, and PRD = 3.25 during independent validation. ANN showed intermediate performance, whereas SVM produced the lowest accuracy. RF-based predictions revealed substantial and spatially heterogeneous variation in SM FC , with values ranging from 13.68 to 43.34, and no simple regional gradient. papers.title: Hydrogeological Modeling of Permeation Grouting: Application to Silicate Grouting from Injection through Degradation
papers.summary: No existing modeling framework seamlessly captures the multi-stage progression of sodium silicate grouting, from initial injection through long-term chemical evolution, at the field scale. We present a modeling framework that integrates numerical simulation with a multi-layer perceptron (MLP) neural network to bridge this gap. The numerical model simulates grout transport during injection and implicitly tracks the transient evolution of soil properties as the gel hardens. Once the injection is complete, a low-permeability barrier forms, controlling groundwater inflow. Barrier degradation is then predicted using an MLP trained on a literature-derived database that relates mass loss to grout composition, hardener type, and soil characteristics. The framework predicts post-injection grout distribution (spatial uniformity, layer thickness, porosity, and hydraulic conductivity) as well as temporal degradation due to syneresis. In a field-scale case study, 340 liters of grout were injected per well across 120 wells, producing an effective influence radius of approximately 0.55 m per well. The resulting low-conductivity layer reduced the average hydraulic conductivity from 0.36 m/hr to 1.3 × 10⁻⁵ m/hr. Peak performance, characterized by the lowest conductivity, was confined to a 2-m-thick zone centered on the injection depth, with conductivity increasing away from the injection points. The framework provides a computational tool for assessing and optimizing grouting strategies in geotechnical and hydraulic engineering, with applications in tunneling, dam construction, and subsurface infrastructure projects.

papers.title: Hydrogeophysical characterization of heterogeneous aeolian dune deposits through integrated ERT, GPR, sedimentological and hydraulic analyses: the Montgrí dune system (NE Spain)
papers.summary: Aeolian dune systems commonly exhibit strong multiscale heterogeneity that controls groundwater flow, moisture distribution, and geophysical responses. This study investigates the stabilized continental dune field of Baix Empordà (NE Spain) through the integration of electrical resistivity tomography (ERT), ground-penetrating radar (GPR), grain-size analysis, and laboratory hydraulic measurements. The dataset comprises seven ERT profiles, 40 GPR profiles, 26 grain-size samples and eight hydraulic conductivity tests. ERT imaging reveals a vertically stratified resistivity structure composed of highly resistive aeolian sands (500–3000 Ω · m) that locally exceed 20 m in thickness, underlain by an intermediate unit (100–400 Ω · m), and finally a laterally continuous conductive basal layer (< 100 Ω · m) interpreted as the transition into the saturated Upper Bartonian detrital sandstone aquifer (ADBS), where water saturation and fine-grained intercalations contribute to the low resistivity. GPR data identify two main radar facies: RF1, characterized by inclined continuous reflectors associated with dune migration and cross-stratification, and RF2, composed of discontinuous concave reflectors related to interdune deposits and erosional surfaces. Sedimentological analyses indicate that dune deposits are coarser (D 50 ≈ 440 μm), better sorted ( σ 1 = 0.55–0.70), and higher hydraulic conductivity (≈ 5.6 × 10 3 cm/day) than interdune deposits (D 50 ≈ 355 μm; σ 1 = 0.71–1.58 and ≈ 2.9 × 10 3 cm/day). Integrated interpretation demonstrates that geophysical signatures are controlled primarily by grain-size distribution, pore connectivity, and moisture retention. The results highlight the strong influence of depositional architecture on subsurface heterogeneity and recharge dynamics, and demonstrate the usefulness of integrated hydrogeophysical approaches for characterizing heterogeneous sandy aquifers and aeolian reservoir analogues.

papers.title: Integrating the multistep flux method for full range soil hydraulic characterisation: from saturation to oven-dryness
papers.summary: Soil hydraulic properties (SHP), defined by the water retention curve (WRC) and the hydraulic conductivity curve (HCC), are crucial to describe water storage and flow in soils. Several methods have been developed and combined to measure these two fundamental curves across the full range from saturation to oven-dryness. However, for the HCC, there is still a data gap for pressure heads between approximately −1 to −100 cm, which is expected to be strongly affected by soil structure. We present an experimental workflow in which the multistep flux (MSF) method is integrated into the well-established combination of methods for measuring SHP, namely the falling head method, the simplified evaporation method, and the dew point method, specially designed to be applied to the same sample. The MSF is an adaptive, direct measurement of the HCC based on applying series of steady-state water flows to a soil sample characterised by unit hydraulic gradient. Once near steady-state flow conditions is achieved, the sample is characterised by a constant pressure head, constant water content and constant unsaturated hydraulic conductivity which is equal to the applied flux. We tested the method for three different soil columns: a repacked sand with a very well-defined air-entry pressure head and two undisturbed silt loams. For the sand, the MSF results coincide with the saturated hydraulic conductivity value, measured with the falling head method. For the undisturbed loam samples, the structural effect on the HCC is clearly visible. Integrating the MSF into the common lab-workflow to characterise SHP will help future studies to investigate soil structure effect on SHP.
