Soil-Structure Interface Behavior Under Unsaturated and Drying Conditions: Experimental Advances and Research Gaps
papers.summary: Soil–structure interface shear behavior plays a fundamental role in the mechanical stability and hydraulic integrity of geotechnical systems, particularly in expansive soils susceptible to desiccation cracking, curling, and permeability changes during seasonal drying. Direct shear testing is widely used to characterize interface behavior; however, conventional configurations often fail to reproduce the coupled hydro-mechanical and thermal conditions associated with drying and restrained shrinkage. This review critically examines advances in modified direct shear apparatuses for investigating soil–structure interfaces, including suction-control techniques based on axis translation and vapor equilibrium, surface-roughness modifications using smooth, grooved, and textured plates, dual-sided configurations, environmental controls, and thermo-hydro-mechanical (THM) adaptations. Experimental findings from natural and artificial soils are synthesized to assess the effects of roughness, drainage, water content, normal stress, matric suction, and temperature on interface shear resistance. Particular attention is given to reported links between peak interface shear resistance and crack initiation in thin-layer desiccation tests, as well as the role of soil–water retention curves in interpreting suction-dependent behavior. Crack initiation mechanisms and THM studies on energy geostructures are discussed. Research gaps include multiscale coupling, testing standardization, and field validation. The review highlights the potential of accessible apparatus modifications to improve interface characterization and predictive modeling under variable climatic conditions.

papers.title: Temporal landslide susceptibility modeling using machine learning: validation against multi-year inventories in the NW Himalayas
papers.summary: The region of Muzaffarabad, located in the tectonically active foothills of the Himalayas, is highly vulnerable to landslides due to frequent slope failures exacerbated by both natural and anthropogenic factors. This study assesses landslide susceptibility and hazard in Muzaffarabad, Azad Jammu and Kashmir, Pakistan, using two machine learning (ML) approaches, specifically Logistic Regression (LR) and Random Forest (RF). A total of thirteen landslide conditioning factors, including topographic, geological, environmental and anthropogenic attributes, were analyzed using models. Landslide susceptibility maps were developed and validated with landslide datasets from 2005, 2007, and 2012, showcasing the models’ predictive performance through accuracy metrics such as Area Under Curve (AUC), Mean Absolute Error (MAE), Root Mean Squared Error (RMSE), F1-score and Kappa. The study found that RF models consistently outperformed LR models in predictive accuracy, with AUC values of 99% for the 2007 dataset and 96.3% for the 2012 dataset. Temporal validation of these models against subsequent-year landslide inventories demonstrated that RF retained stronger predictive stability over time than LR, although the use of static conditioning layers limits the interpretation of these temporal changes as direct evidence of landscape dynamics. The results underscore the potential of RF-based models for operational landslide hazard assessments, providing critical insights for hazard mitigation and urban planning in tectonically active regions. The study’s findings contribute to the development of more effective risk management strategies, particularly in the face of ongoing seismic activity and climate change, enhancing regional resilience to landslide disasters.

papers.title: HydroUK: Soil Hydraulic Property Prediction Tool
papers.summary: HydroUK uses machine learning to predict soil hydraulic properties from sand, silt, clay, bulk density, and saturated volumetric water content. The predicted parameters are used in the van Genuchten equation to generate a soil-water characteristic curve (SWCC), which describes how soil water content changes with matric suction. Saturated hydraulic conductivity is predicted separately.

Longitudinal Dynamic Response of End-Bearing Piles in Radially Heterogeneous Unsaturated Soil
papers.summary: This study investigates the longitudinal dynamic response of end-bearing piles embedded in radially heterogeneous unsaturated soil induced by construction disturbance. The unsaturated soil is described using the theory of motion for three-phase poroelastic media, while the radial inhomogeneity of the surrounding soil is represented by the complex shear stiffness transfer model. The soil is discretized into concentric vertical annular zones, each of which is assumed to be homogeneous, while soil properties may differ between adjacent zones. The governing equations for each soil zone are then solved and coupled with the pile governing equation to derive an analytical solution for the pile-head complex impedance. After validating the proposed solution, a parametric analysis is conducted to examine how pile–soil parameters affect the longitudinal dynamic response of end-bearing piles in radially heterogeneous unsaturated soil.

papers.title: Mechanistically informed statistical modeling of hydraulic performance for bentonite construction liners: long-term mechanistic insights from real-time data, ANOVA, and regression analysis
papers.summary: Sand–bentonite liners (SBLs) play a pivotal role in geotechnical and environmental engineering as hydraulic barriers designed to minimize contaminant migration and safeguard subsurface soil and groundwater. This study presents a comprehensive statistical investigation into the key operational, field, and climatic factors influencing the long-term durability and hydraulic efficiency of compacted SBLs under sustained flow conditions. A long-term laboratory permeability test was conducted to maintain continuous flow through the specimen while systematically monitoring the effects of aging, hydraulic head variation, cumulative flow, and ambient temperature. Quantitative evaluation using one- and two-way ANOVA, interaction plots, and a quadratic regression model (F = 324.20, p < 0.001) revealed that cumulative flow and aging, along with their interaction, exerted the most pronounced influence on hydraulic conductivity. Specifically, hydraulic conductivity increased by approximately 38% after 90 days of sustained flow, which highlights the critical role of cumulative seepage in permeability evolution. These findings provide valuable quantitative insights into mechanisms governing the long-term behavior of SBLs and offer a data-driven foundation for designing more sustainable and efficient barrier designs.

papers.title: Mechanism of shallow hard-shell-layer formation for newly-reclaimed dredged silt using vacuum dewatering combined with preloading
papers.summary: Newly-reclaimed dredged silt sites present a critical geotechnical challenge immediately after hydraulic filling. The ground surface remains as fluidized mud, preventing personnel and equipment access, yet conventional treatment methods assume the site is already accessible. This paper proposes a vacuum dewatering combined with preloading (VDCP) method for rapid formation of a shallow hard-shell layer without sand cushions or prolonged drying. A three-dimensional horizontal–vertical drainage network is established, coupling free-water extraction and negative-pressure consolidation. Physical model tests on Xiamen dredged silt (initial water content 281%) and Plaxis 2D numerical simulations are conducted to investigate the reinforcement mechanisms during the hard-shell formation stage. After 1,188 h of vacuum extraction, the average water content of the shallow soil decreases to 58%, the void ratio reduces from 7.53 to 1.49, and the ultimate bearing capacity increases from near zero to over 40 kPa, meeting the requirements for personnel and light machinery access. Numerical comparisons demonstrate that the three-dimensional drainage system achieves approximately 61.0% excess pore water pressure dissipation within 1,200 h, compared with 22.4% for horizontal-only and 18.3% for vertical-only drainage, confirming the synergistic effect of combined drainage channels, although these ratios are semi-quantitative. A consolidation coupling effect between vacuum and surcharge is observed; however, surcharge should be applied only after the soil has gained sufficient shear strength. The VDCP method and the proposed phased treatment framework, which designates shallow hard-shell formation as an independent preliminary stage with explicit transition criteria, provide a feasible technical pathway for similar projects that require priority construction of working platforms before deep reinforcement.

papers.title: Long-Duration Creep Behavior of Compacted Edmonton Clays: Effects of Relative Compaction, Water Content, and Plasticity
papers.source: ERA: Education and Research Archive (University of Alberta)
papers.summary: Compacted clays are widely used in road embankments, railway subgrades, levees, and many other infrastructure projects. In regions such as Alberta, compacted clay fills are subjected to long-term loading and seasonal moisture variations, which may result in creep deformation and long-term settlement, posing challenges to infrastructure serviceability. Previous studies on creep behaviour of cohesive soils have mainly focused on saturated soils, whereas research on compacted unsaturated fine-grained soils remains limited. Further, creep studies of unsaturated clay in the literature are characterized by relatively short testing durations ranging from several days to one or two weeks. Longer durations are required to obtain reliable results to guide practice. In this study, long-duration creep tests were conducted on two types of compacted soils obtained from Edmonton, including a low- to intermediate-plasticity clay (classification CL–CI) and a high-plasticity clay (CH). The effects of stress level, relative compaction, soil plasticity, initial water content and moisture change on the long-term deformation behaviour of compacted unsaturated soils were investigated. In addition, consolidation behaviour under saturated conditions was compared with the unsaturated creep behaviour. Vertical stresses ranging from 50 to 400 kPa were applied during the long-duration creep tests, which were performed under sealed high-humidity conditions with a relatively constant temperature of approximately 20 ℃ and relative humidity exceeding 99%. Test durations ranged from approximately 3 to 11 weeks, substantially longer than those commonly reported in previous creep studies of unsaturated clays. Under unsaturated conditions, both the CL–CI and CH soils exhibited continuous creep deformation accompanied by water uptake during long-term loading, with equilibrium water contents ranging from approximately 19% to 23% for the CL–CI soil and 28% to 38% for the CH soil. papers.title: An analytical, single parameter model of falling-head ponded infiltration
papers.summary: In this study, an analytical model is developed of the water-level dynamics of a temporary surface pond formed by sudden flooding of initially unsaturated soil. Pond-depth evolution is governed by infiltration and a constant evaporation rate. The model couples a surface-water balance equation with a linearized Richards equation, assuming constant hydraulic conductivity and specific moisture capacity. Although subsurface water transport is described by conventional Fickian diffusion, the coupling introduces a temporal memory kernel into the reduced equation governing pond depth, giving rise to effective non-Fickian relaxation dynamics. The resulting semi-infinite analytical solution is expressed in terms of the scaled complementary error function, which corresponds to a fractional relaxation function with an algebraic asymptote. The solution also allows the characteristic pond-emptying time to be determined. The analytical model is evaluated against numerical integration of the nonlinear Richards equation using van Genuchten–Mualem hydraulic properties of sandy loam, loam, and clay loam soils. The model reproduces the simulated pond-depth evolution with good accuracy ($R^2 > 0.95$ in all investigated cases). For hydrostatic initial conditions, only the product of hydraulic conductivity and specific moisture capacity is identifiable. The fitted parameter decreases systematically with groundwater table depth, following an approximate power-law scaling relationship with the initial pressure-head difference. The overall results demonstrate how effective non-Fickian dynamics can emerge from coupled Fickian transport processes and provide a computationally inexpensive description of nonlinear infiltration dynamics

papers.title: Estimation and Modeling of Groundwater Contaminants in Uttarakhand's state
papers.source: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.summary: The Himalayan State of Uttarakhand in northern India relies heavily on groundwater to meet the drinking water and agricultural needs. However, rapid urbanization, industrial activities, and irrigation practices have led to increased contamination of groundwater resources. The quality of both surface water and groundwater in Uttarakhand is deteriorating due to developmental activities, geological factors, and the mixing of industrial wastes. The harmful toxic metal ions such as arsenic, cadmium, chromium, and lead have been detected in drinking water sources across most districts of the state. Among these contaminants, lead has been found to be detrimental to health health. Lead, a potent neurotoxin, poses severe health risks, especially through contaminated drinking water and food. In children, lead exposure can cause cognitive impairment, learning disabilities, and behavioral disorders, while in adults, prolonged exposure increases the risk of hypertension, cardiovascular diseases, kidney damage, and reproductive complications. The movement of lead in regional groundwater systems occurs through unsaturated porous media, where preferential flow pathways significantly influence the distribution of soil water content and solute concentrations. The toxicological effects of lead ions have been assessed through laboratory experiments based on the stipulated limits recommended by the Bureau of Indian Standards (BIS) and the World Health Organization (WHO). To better understand the extent of lead contamination, this study numerically develops regional transport models to estimate the movement of lead contaminants in both spatial and temporal domains. The findings aim to provide insights into the transport dynamics of lead in groundwater and support the formulation of effective mitigation strategies for safeguarding water quality in Uttarakhand.

Overall and Local Effects of Multi-Temporal Imagery on Rainfall-Induced Landslide Mapping
papers.summary: Higher overall accuracy does not necessarily mean more complete landslide mapping at every location. Across eight rainfall-related events, we examine the benefits of earlier satellite imagery using U-TAE, a neural network that combines images acquired on different dates, as the main model. We compare overall accuracy with the fraction of mapped landslide area detected within local image patches. Mean average precision increased from 0.333 with a post-event image to 0.379 with a pre/post pair and 0.419 with a longer sequence. Adding earlier images to the pair improved mean average precision in seven events but slightly reduced it in Chimanimani. However, the average increase in the detected fraction across locations and regions was 1.1 percentage points (95% interval −1.3 to +3.3). This provides no clear evidence that earlier images increased the average fraction of mapped landslide area detected. The estimated gain in Italy decreased from 3.0 to 0.3 percentage points when the decision thresholds changed, indicating that the apparent improvement depended on how the predictions were converted into a landslide map. The benefit of earlier images was also greater in patches containing more mapped landslide area in some regions, but was not clearly related to the strength of surface change in patches with sufficient mapped area and usable optical observations. An auxiliary comparison with U-Net, a convolutional image-segmentation model, also showed local detection differences alongside higher overall accuracy. Local detection also varied when the same models were retrained using unchanged images. Checking local detection changes alongside conventional accuracy measures helps assess whether adding earlier imagery reduces missed landslide area across locations.

papers.summary: Landslide segmentation from multitemporal imagery must retain sparse scars and irregular boundaries. Efficient repeated mapping also requires models with manageable computation and storage. We use a 21-channel input design combining pre- and post-event reflectance, their differences, terrain and validity. We propose detail–context adaptive pruning (DCAP), which optimizes learnable channel scaling factors (gates) shared across dependency groups under a computation budget and recovers pruned models with task-aware losses. Evaluation uses model ensembles on 990 training, 132 validation and 198 test chips from Nepal in 2017–2019, separated by whole spatial groups. Under common task-aware recovery, the proposed method reduced multiply–accumulate operations (MACs) by 70.03% and parameters by 88.56%, while validation average precision (AP) and Dice increased from 0.4900/0.5154 to 0.4949/0.5238. On test, AP was 0.4268, a 0.65-percentage-point decrease, whereas Dice reached 0.4791, a 0.31-percentage-point increase. Joint bootstrap support was 1.0000 on validation. Small-component uncertainty limited DCAP’s test support to 0.9484, below the required 0.95; Group Taylor reached 85.11% MAC reduction under the validation rule, with test support 0.7933. Loss ablations showed endpoint-specific contributions and trade-offs. Geographic validation achieved 54.21% chip-weighted MAC reduction with inner-selected models, including dense fallback in the west. FP32 CUDA Graphs reduced DCAP latency by 34.1% on RTX 4080 and 32.5% on Jetson AGX Orin. These findings support substantial compression with small aggregate-score changes within the sampled population, while transfer to independent events has not been established.

papers.summary: Data-driven models have increasingly dominated landslide susceptibility mapping, yet regional studies often rely on coarse-resolution data and uninterpretable architectures. This study proposes a geomorphologically constrained, dual-branch deep learning framework to predict rainfall-induced landslides in the Tyrolean Alps, bridging the gap between empirical algorithms and topographic determinism. To capture regional moisture dynamics, 30-day continuous antecedent precipitation sequences from reanalysis data were fused with highly localized 5-m resolution morphometric derivatives. The model was evaluated using strict spatial cross-validation to account for spatial autocorrelation, and an integrated gradients framework was applied to achieve interpretability. The model achieved a robust, spatially validated performance, quantitatively revealing a delayed hydrological response where antecedent rainfall serves as a critical prerequisite for landslide initiation. Furthermore, a geomorphological constraint (slopes ≤15° = 0 probability) successfully eliminated false-positive artifacts in valley bottoms. These results demonstrate that integrating regional dynamic meteorological memory with high-resolution topographic constraints is essential for identifying micro-scale structural traps, paving the way for advanced predictive hazard assessments.

Evaluating the Geological and Soil Characteristics Influencing Landslide Susceptibility in Anambra State, Nigeria
papers.source: RESEARCH JOURNAL OF PURE SCIENCE AND TECHNOLOGY
papers.summary: This study investigates soil erodibility in three Local Government Areas (LGAs) within Anambra State, Nigeria—Ekwusigo, Ihiala, and Ogbaru—situated in the lower Niger River Basin prone to frequent and severe flooding. The aim is to assess geological and soil characteristics influencing landslide susceptibility. The methodology involves identifying and characterizing soil types, calculating the Soil Erodibility Factor (K) using empirical formulas, and mapping erosion susceptibility. Data from the Soil Map of the World (version 3.6) were used, corrected for accuracy, and integrated into geographic projections. Analysis included William’s equation to calculate K factors based on soil properties such as sand, silt, clay, and organic matter content. Results highlight diverse geological formations: Ameki Group (34.24%), Benin Formation (0.26%), Ogwashi-Asaba Formation (1.59%), River Niger (1.86%), Sands, Gravels, and Clay (42.36%), and Sombreiro Warri Deltaic Plain (19.69%). Soil types identified include Dystric Nitosols (K = 0.0178) covering 449.11 km² and Gleysols (K = 0.0189) covering 283.95 km², each exhibiting unique erosion susceptibilities. Gleysols are characterized by poor drainage and high-water retention, posing higher landslide risks during heavy rainfall compared to Dystric Nitosols. The correlation between K factors and hydrological data, showing Gleysols as more vulnerable to landslides in wet conditions. Recommendations include targeted erosion control measures like terracing, vegetative buffers, and improved drainage systems for high-risk zones. Maintaining vegetative cover and implementing sustainable land management practices are crucial for mitigating erosion and landslide risks. This study provides a detailed understanding of geological and soil factors affecting landslide susceptibility in Anambra State. It underscores the need for tailored soil conservation and landslide mitigation strategies aligned with specific geological formations and soil type

papers.title: Spatio‐Temporal Modelling of Extreme Rainfall Occurrence in Brazil
papers.summary: ABSTRACT Extreme rainfall events are major hydroclimatic hazards in Brazil, causing floods, landslides, infrastructure damage, and agricultural losses across distinct climatic regions. This study develops a Bayesian spatio‐temporal Log‐Gaussian Cox Process (LGCP) framework to model the occurrence of extreme precipitation using CHIRPS daily rainfall data. The results reveal clear differences between moderate‐extreme and ultra‐extreme rainfall regimes. Lower thresholds are strongly influenced by seasonal forcing associated with the South American Monsoon System, whereas the most severe events exhibit stronger temporal dependence, episodic clustering, and more localized spatial organization, indicating increasingly persistent spatio‐temporal structures in the latent risk field as precipitation intensity increases. Regional decompositions further show substantial heterogeneity in trends, seasonality, and persistence across Brazil, reflecting the influence of distinct hydroclimatic regimes and atmospheric processes. The estimated latent spatial fields identify persistent high‐risk corridors over the Amazon basin, southeastern coastal Brazil, and southern subtropical regions. Overall, the findings suggest that extreme rainfall occurrence in Brazil is governed by multiple interacting regional processes whose persistence and spatial organization may evolve under climate variability and climate change.

papers.summary: Abstract Separated analyses are widely used to evaluate the stability of slopes after rainfall and earthquakes. However, the combined impact of rainfall infiltration and earthquake shaking on slope stability remains insufficiently studied. Therefore, a unique closed-form analytical solution to calculate the factor of safety (FS) for homogeneous unsaturated slopes under combined seepage and seismic forces has been proposed by modifying the conventional Bishop’s method. The two-dimensional seepage pattern was considered to capture rainfall infiltration, while pseudo-dynamic forces at each failure slice accounted for earthquake shaking. Further, an analytical search method was developed to locate the critical slip surface. Additionally, a coupled hydromechanical finite-element model was used to analyze rainfall-induced seepage, deformation, and stress redistribution. The resulting slope condition was further evaluated under seismic loading to represent rainfall–earthquake effects without implying full two-way coupling between infiltration and earthquake shaking. All these newly proposed methodologies were applied to the 2014 Malin landslide in Maharashtra, India, to replicate the landslide mechanism and identify root causes to show the application of proposed analytical solutions. A comparison with field observations and literature demonstrated that both the analytical and numerical models realistically represented the Malin landslide. Further, the proposed analytical model was validated against a numerical analysis of a real earthquake-induced landslide. The models accurately reproduced the onset, failure zone, and progression of instability over time. The present study provides the application of new analytical solutions for practical landslides, additionally offering a reference for prevention and evacuation plans.

papers.summary: Buried oil and gas pipelines crossing landslide-prone terrain are vulnerable to large ground deformation, yet their progressive pipe–soil interaction and failure behavior remain insufficiently characterized experimentally. This study investigates the mechanical response and failure of a shallow-buried steel pipeline subjected to lateral landslide loading using large-scale physical model tests. The experiment comprised sequential slope inclination adjustments in 5° increments, followed by displacement-controlled loading at a slope inclination of 30°, while pipeline axial strain, surrounding soil pressure, and deflection were monitored. The results show that increasing slope inclination intensified strain concentration near the pipeline midspan. During displacement loading, the tensile strain peaked at approximately 8100 με at a landslide displacement of 50 mm, whereas the compressive strain reached approximately −12,400 με at 58 mm. Frontal soil pressure peaked earlier, at approximately 44–45 kPa near 46 mm displacement, indicating that peak soil resistance preceded pipeline instability. Local buckling subsequently developed near the pipeline midspan, accompanied by approximately symmetric beam-like global bending. Comparisons with a PSI soil-spring model and a three-dimensional solid-contact finite-element model showed reasonable agreement during the pre-buckling response but substantial underestimation of strain after local buckling, with predicted values less than half the measured magnitude. These findings clarify the transition from soil-resistance-controlled deformation to localized structural instability and provide experimental evidence for evaluating buried pipelines subjected to landslide-induced ground deformation.

papers.summary: Abstract Landslides are among the most destructive natural hazards, causing substantial loss of life and infrastructure, particularly in mountainous regions. Accurate identification of landslide-prone areas remains challenging due to complex and nonlinear interactions among geological, topographical, and environmental factors. This study evaluates kernel-based machine learning approaches, namely, kernel logistic regression (KLR) and support vector machine (SVM), for landslide susceptibility mapping (LSM) in Sikkim, India. A balanced data set comprising 693 landslide and 695 nonlandslide samples was constructed using 15 conditioning factors representing topographic, hydrological, environmental, geological, and seismic conditions. The grid search method was utilized to identify optimal hyperparameter configurations. Model performance was quantitatively assessed using accuracy, kappa coefficient, specificity, area under curve (AUC), landslide density, and success rate curve (SRC). The results demonstrate that the KLR with a polynomial kernel (KLR_poly) achieved the highest predictive performance, with an accuracy of 0.741 and an area under curve (AUC) of 0.829, outperforming other KLR variants, while the SVM with an rbf kernel (SVM_rbf) achieved the highest predictive performance, with an accuracy of 0.749 and an AUC of 0.764, outperforming other SVM variants. Furthermore, the landslide density analysis showed a systematic increase in landslide concentration from low to high susceptibility classes for nonlinear models, while SRC results indicated moderate to good predictive capability across all models, confirming effective spatial prioritization of landslide-prone areas. Additionally, a feature importance analysis was conducted to identify the most significant factors influencing landslide occurrence.

papers.summary: Landslides are one of the most destructive natural hazards. In highway construction, cut slopes are particularly prone to instability and failure because excavation disturbs the original stress state. Monitoring slope stability and issuing early warnings can effectively prevent casualties and mitigate losses. Traditional slope monitoring relies mainly on surface displacement and other external deformation measurements, which are relatively insensitive to internal damage preceding visible failure. In this study, we conducted a monitoring experiment on a cut slope in Hangzhou, Zhejiang Province, using ambient noise interferometry, which provides a continuous, non-invasive means of monitoring relative seismic velocity changes (dv/v) that reflect the internal stiffness state of the slope. Velocity changes were obtained by stacking long-duration cross-correlations of ambient noise. However, frequent rainfall severely degraded the reconstruction of Green’s functions from such cross-correlations. To address this issue, we propose a sparse non-negative matrix factorization (NMF) method to suppress rainfall-induced noise and obtain more stable Green’s functions for high-resolution dv/v measurements. The obtained dv/v series exhibited a clear 24 h periodicity consistent with temperature variations, and the seismic velocity decreased by approximately 6% from 9 to 10 August, coinciding with typhoon landfall and heavy rainfall on 9 August. Following the drop in velocity, the inclinometer of the three-component geophone recorded a noticeable slip, and the agreement among the velocity drop, the slip, and field-observed cracks indicates that velocity variations retrieved from ambient noise can effectively reflect the internal stiffness weakening of the cut slope. By integrating the proposed method with other deformation measurements, landslide early warning for cut slopes can be improved.

papers.summary: Abstract Heavy rainfall is a common natural phenomenon. Regarding the issue of water infiltration in an infinite vegetated slope (consisting of rooted and unrooted layers) under the heavy rainfall condition, the infiltration process is divided into two stages— before and after the slope surface reaches saturation—and the corresponding analytical solutions are acquired through several mathematical approaches. Then the proposed solutions are effectively verified by two comparisons. Finally, based on the factor of safety ( F s ), the effects of key factors on the slope’s shallow stability are quantitatively investigated, and some novel findings are obtained. For example, an increased heavy rainfall rate reduces the F s , but this effect exhibits a tendency of increasing and then decreasing. An increase in transpiration rate enhances the infinite vegetated slope’s whole stability, while its influence will be declined after the heavy rainfall infiltration. The increased root tensile strength improves the F s within the rooted layer, but does not affect the unrooted layer’s stability. Moreover, compared with the “exponential” root shape, the F s within the unrooted layer is slightly lower in the case of the “uniform” root shape. Overall, the findings provide useful insights into infiltration mechanisms and shallow stability of infinite vegetated slopes under heavy rainfalls.

papers.summary: Abstract Groundwater seepage is influenced by various anthropogenic factors during urban construction, among which subsurface structures and surface hardening are two key factors. This study employed numerical simulations to investigate the impacts of rainfall infiltration on groundwater seepage under the effect of urban construction. A numerical model was established to predict groundwater level (GWL) in the phreatic aquifer (Aq0), incorporating the actual distribution of impervious surfaces and subsurface structures for a representative urban area in Shanghai. The model accounted for land surface conditions through rainfall infiltration coefficients, while subsurface structures were parameterized using equivalent hydraulic conductivity ( K eq ) derived from effective medium theory. Validation results show that the model achieved a maximum error of only 1.7%, demonstrating reliable performance in predicting groundwater seepage. There is 23.23% area with GWL declining more than 0.4 m in the actual scenario with 93% impervious surface hardening comparing without surface hardening. Prediction scenarios with varying reduction rates of impervious surface compared with the actual scenario ( R a ) were conducted to investigate the impact of surface hardening on GWL. The results indicate average GWL of the study area presents exponential decay with the impervious surface ratio. Further, the variations in GWL of Aq0 were investigated by reducing hardened surfaces in different locations with the same R a . As the proportion of underground structures in the reduced impervious surface increases, the area with the same increment of GWL decreases. Prioritizing low impact development in areas with lower subsurface structure density can significantly enhance the efficiency of groundwater recharge by rainfall infiltration.

papers.summary: Decisions regarding mitigation and adaptation in terms of money in areas prone to landslides need to be made repeatedly. But, there is no evidence of how incentive structures of disaster insurance affect the mitigation process in dynamic environments of hazard. In the present study, mitigation and insurance decisions were studied using the Interactive Landslide Simulator, a microworld of Human Factors involving repeated decision-making under landslide risk. Seventy-five participants hailing from landslide-prone areas of Himachal Pradesh, India, were randomly allocated into No Insurance, Benevolent Insurance, or Smart Insurance groups and asked to perform 36 rounds of decision-making. While the highest level of mitigation was observed in case of no insurance, Smart Insurance resulted in maximum insurance investment but did not enhance mitigation over Benevolent Insurance. Findings suggest that reimbursement-system design can shape risk-management behavior in disaster-risk policy.

Additionally, a comprehensive parametric study has been conducted to evaluate the effects of transient flow and elevated temperature on the uplift capacity of shallow strip plate anchors. The results indicate that the behavior of plate anchors in unsaturated sand and silt is distinctly different from that in clay.

papers.summary: Abstract The paper focuses on the effect of the vertical ground acceleration component on slope stability. The proposed stability method is based on Newmark’s sliding block concept, which provides an intuitive indicator of slope stability. Contrary to the original Newmark method, both components of excitations, tangent and normal to the slip plane, are considered in force equilibrium. In the paper, the extended Newmark method is coupled with dynamic response obtained using the FEM and a direct time-integration scheme. Coupling the simple stability approach with the stress distribution history eliminates uncertainty in determining the intensity of the dynamic load acting on the sliding block. In the coupled method, the equilibrium of the sliding and resisting forces is considered along the discretized slip plane. When the limit equilibrium is reached, the relative movement of the block begins, and the permanent displacement of a sliding mass is accumulated. The influence of excitation components on permanent displacement is examined using a uniform steep slope as an example. The presented results indicate that shallow deformation mechanisms are more strongly affected by inertial forces than deeper ones. In the analyzed cases, the peak average acceleration for the shallow mechanism was between 1.2 and 3.0 times that for the deep mechanism. Furthermore, the effect of vertical acceleration on permanent displacements is notably more significant in shallow failure modes. It is shown that the permanent displacement obtained by the original Newmark’s method can be 74.3% lower than that obtained by the extended Newmark’s method. The impact of vertical acceleration itself can reach 24.6%.

papers.summary: Abstract Probabilistic stability analysis of soil slopes is essential for reliable geotechnical design due to pronounced uncertainties in soil strength and hydraulic parameters. Although crude Monte Carlo simulation (MCS) provides a robust benchmark, its prohibitive computational cost and the limitations of gradient-based methods such as FORM and SORM in handling nonlinear and non-Gaussian performance functions restrict their practical applicability. To address these challenges, this study conducts a comparative analysis of advanced surrogate-based reliability methods, specifically polynomial chaos expansion–enhanced Monte Carlo simulation (PCE-MCS) and kriging-enhanced Monte Carlo simulation (K-MCS), against traditional gradient-based methods such as the first-order reliability method (FORM) and second-order reliability method (SORM) for evaluating the stability of unsaturated finite soil slopes. papers.summary: Abstract Landslides are among the most significant natural hazards in the Himalayan region of India, causing substantial damage to infrastructure, natural resources, and local communities. This study presents an integrated hydro-geotechnical approach for regional landslide susceptibility assessment by combining statistical susceptibility mapping with slope stability evaluation. The proposed framework considers the influence of key hydrologic factors, including rainfall, drainage density, topographic wetness, and groundwater conditions, together with geotechnical properties to better explain the mechanisms controlling slope failure. Five bivariate statistical models, namely, frequency ratio (FR), information value (IV), weight of evidence (WoE), certainty factor (CF), and Shannon entropy (SE), were applied to produce landslide susceptibility maps. Their performance was evaluated using the area under the curve (AUC) and landslide density index (LDI). Among the evaluated models, SE achieved the highest predictive accuracy ( AUC = 87.17 % ), followed closely by FR (87.06%). The results indicate that steep slopes ( > 30 ° ), weak lithological formations, high drainage density, and groundwater conditions are the main factors controlling landslide occurrence in the study area. Slope stability was further evaluated using laboratory-derived geotechnical parameters and circular failure charts (CFC), providing an independent assessment of slope conditions under different groundwater scenarios. The combined use of statistical modeling, hydrologic factors, and geotechnical verification improves the reliability of landslide susceptibility assessment and provides a practical framework that can be applied in other mountainous regions affected by rainfall-induced landslides.

papers.title: Response and stability analysis of soil organic carbon in different ecosystems of China under climate warming gradient scenarios
papers.summary: Under the background of global warming, the response pattern of soil organic carbon (SOC) and the stability of carbon sinks have received more and more attention. This research adopts the Space-for-time substitution (SFTS) method to build a spatial unit that integrates climate, vegetation and land use factors. These units are used to analyze the SOC spatial distribution patterns along the warming gradients in different regions of China and their related variability. Through linear regression, machine learning and neighborhood least squares fitting, the main driving factors of SOC space changes on multiple scales have been determined. The results show that SOC has a strong correlation with temperature and presents a nonlinear pattern in a higher temperature range. In most areas, the initial SOC content is the dominant factor related to SOC changes, and its constraint effect increases with the increase of soil depth. In contrast, vegetation coverage and precipitation show a stronger correlation on the surface, and there is obvious regional heterogeneity. In areas with low initial carbon content, high vegetation coverage and good moisture conditions, the estimated SOC increase is often greater. With the increase of temperature and soil depth, the content of organic carbon in the soil gradually decreases, and the area of high-content areas gradually shrinks. By establishing a spatial analysis framework that combines ecological units and environmental gradients, this study enhances the regional understanding of SOC change patterns and provides a scientific basis for assessing the distribution of soil carbon in China and formulating regional management strategies. These results should be interpreted as a general response patterns, rather than an accurate prediction of the future SOC dynamics.

papers.summary: Soil moisture regimes result from interactions between climate and soil properties and are key determinants of ecosystem functioning and vegetation distribution. However, climate change assessments commonly rely on gridded climate data that may overlook local soil heterogeneity. This study evaluates how pedodiversity within a single climate grid cell influences projected soil moisture regimes (SMRs) in a Mediterranean vineyard landscape in central Spain. Twenty-four soil profiles were characterized through field and laboratory analyses, identifying seven taxonomic subgroups with available water capacity (AWC) values ranging from 32 to 133 mm, subsequently represented by four levels (41, 64, 74, and 111 mm). SMRs were simulated using the Java Newhall Simulation Model, driven by historical climate data and six EURO-CORDEX regional climate projections under RCP4.5 and RCP8.5 for 2030–2059 and 2050–2079. Xeric conditions predominated, but soil-specific AWC modified both long-term SMR classifications and annual regime frequencies under identical climatic forcing. Under historical conditions, the highest soil-specific AWC (111 mm) led to classification as Dry Xeric, whereas soils with lower AWC values (41–74 mm) were classified as Typic Xeric. Future projections altered the relative occurrence of Ustic, Typic Xeric, Dry Xeric, and Aridic conditions, with responses varying among AWC levels, climate models, scenarios, and projection periods. Importantly, decreasing AWC did not produce a simple monotonic shift toward drier regimes. These results demonstrate that soil water-storage variability associated with pedodiversity modulates the local expression of climate change and should be considered into soil-climate impact assessments.

papers.summary: Gedangsari District, Gunungkidul Regency, is an area with potential landslide susceptibility due to its physical characteristics, which are influenced by slope gradient, rainfall, rock types, soil types, and land use. This study aims to (1) map landslide susceptibility levels in Gedangsari District, Gunungkidul Regency, and (2) determine priority areas for mitigation based on landslide susceptibility levels. The analysis was conducted using a Geographic Information System (GIS) with spatial data comprising slope gradient, rainfall, rock types, soil types, and land use. The data were processed using the Weighted Overlay method with the assistance of ArcGIS Pro software. The results show that the study area is predominantly classified as having high landslide susceptibility, covering 37.303 km² or 55.25% of the total area. The moderate susceptibility class covers 30.085 km² or 44.56%, while the low susceptibility class covers 0.125 km² or 0.19%. Based on this classification, areas with high susceptibility are designated as Priority I, areas with moderate susceptibility as Priority II, and areas with low susceptibility as Priority III. The predominance of the high susceptibility class indicates that most of the areas identified through the classification require attention in landslide mitigation efforts. The resulting susceptibility map is expected to serve as a source of spatial information and a reference for regional planning and the determination of landslide mitigation priorities in Gedangsari District, Gunungkidul Regency.

papers.summary: Sawangan District in Magelang Regency is an area prone to landslides due to topographic conditions and environmental characteristics that facilitate their occurrence. Situated between Mount Merapi and Mount Merbabu, the region features varying slope gradients, unconsolidated volcanic materials, and relatively high rainfall. This study aims to analyze landslide susceptibility levels for 2025 and the probability of landslide occurrence in Sawangan District during the 2024–2025 period. A descriptivequantitative method was employed, utilizing a spatial analysis approach specifically overlay and scoring techniques alongside binary logistic regression analysis to determine landslide probability values. Sampling was conducted using a purposive sampling method based on five environmental parameters and recorded landslide locations. The research results indicate that Sawangan District is categorized into four landslide susceptibility classes: not susceptible, slightly susceptible, susceptible, and highly susceptible. Binary logistic regression analysis reveals that landslide probability falls into four classes low, moderate, high, and very high, with an AUC value of 0.846, demonstrating the model's good discriminative ability in distinguishing between landslide and non-landslide locations. While landslide occurrences are predominantly found in the susceptible and highly susceptible classes, some incidents also occurred in the slightly susceptible and not susceptible classes. These findings indicate that landslides can occur across various levels of susceptibility and slope gradients; therefore, vigilance is required not only in areas with high susceptibility but also in those with lower susceptibility. papers.summary: The conversion of forest land to agricultural land can alter vegetation cover and affect slope stability. This study aims to identify changes in land cover and map landslide risk levels in Kempo Subdistrict, Dompu Regency. The study employed a descriptive quantitative approach based on Geographic Information Systems (GIS). Secondary data used included land cover, rainfall, slope gradient, soil type, and administrative boundaries. Analysis was conducted through classification, scoring, weighting, and parameter overlay using QGIS. The results of the study show changes in land cover during the observation period, particularly an increase in the area of dryland agriculture from 7,594.37 ha in 2017 to 9,729.13 ha in 2021, while scrubland decreased from 3,029.54 ha to 1,382.39 ha. Landslide risk mapping identified three classes: low, moderate, and high. High-risk zones are primarily associated with hilly areas, steep to very steep slopes, Lithosol soils, relatively high rainfall, and land cover that has been converted to agricultural or open land. These results can serve as supporting information for land management and landslide mitigation in Kempo Subdistrict. Field validation and data alignment are necessary to improve the accuracy of the results.

papers.source: Open Access Victoria University of Wellington | Te Herenga Waka (Figshare)
papers.summary: Landslide dams, formed when landslide debris blocks a river, occur across Aotearoa New Zealand. These events pose serious hazards to downstream communities and infrastructure, as sudden breaches can result in unexpected flooding and debris flows. They are also important components of complex cascading slope-river systems. Despite their contribution to sediment cascades and potential flood hazard, they remain under-researched. Understanding the interactions between hydrological, geological, and climatic factors governing landslide dam evolution is crucial for hazard management planning. The Tairāwhiti Gisborne region on the East Coast of Aotearoa New Zealand is prone to landslides and subsequent dams, due to its steep slopes, susceptible lithology, and exposure to tropical storms from the east. Despite this vulnerability, very little is known about the material properties and behaviour of landslide dams in this area. The primary aim of this thesis was to investigate the geomorphic and geotechnical aspects of dams in the Tairāwhiti Gisborne region, to understand their formation and breach processes. Three elements of analyses were used to investigate these landslide dams. Each landslide source and deposit were mapped as polygons, using aerial imagery between 1988 and 2023. Second, the short-term evolution of the Waiorongomai and Tiniroto landslide dams was documented through a series of engineering geomorphic maps, using LiDAR and aerial imagery in ArcGIS Pro. papers.summary: Rainfall-induced slope instability is one of the most critical geotechnical hazards worldwide, causing significant damage to infrastructure and loss of life. Predicting slope stability under rainfall conditions remains challenging due to the complex interaction between soil properties, slope geometry, and transient hydrological processes. This research addresses this challenge by developing a reliable and practical predictive framework that integrates experimental investigation, numerical modeling, and machine learning. The study was conducted in three sequential stages. First, geotechnical centrifuge tests were performed at the University of Western Ontario to investigate slope response under controlled rainfall conditions. A calibrated rainfall simulation system ensured uniform and repeatable rainfall application, while slope deformation and pore water pressures were monitored to understand failure mechanisms. Second, numerical simulations using SEEP/W and SLOPE/W were conducted to evaluate slope stability across a wide range of conditions, including different soil types (clay, silt, and sand), slope geometries, and rainfall scenarios. This process generated a comprehensive dataset of 21,438 cases. Finally, machine learning models, including Multiple Linear Regression, Random Forest, and Extra Trees, were developed to predict the factor of safety using seven input variables. The Extra Trees model showed the highest predictive accuracy and strong generalization capability, particularly under unseen slope geometries. The results also highlight the importance of including rainfall intensity and duration in predictive models. The developed model was implemented into a web-based early warning system capable of providing rapid predictions. This research contributes to improved hazard assessment and supports the development of practical tools for geotechnical risk mitigation.

papers.summary: Landslides are processes involving the downslope movement of soil and/or rock masses due to slope instability. Wonogiri Regency exhibits diverse topographic, rainfall, geological, land-use, and soil characteristics, resulting in varying levels of landslide susceptibility across the region. This study aims to analyze the spatial distribution of landslide susceptibility levels and their correspondence with actual landslide occurrences in Wonogiri Regency. A quantitative method was employed using a Geographic Information System (GIS) approach via the Weighted Overlay method. The parameters utilized included rainfall, slope gradient, geology, land use, and soil type. Each parameter was assigned a score and weight, followed by an overlay process to generate a landslide susceptibility map. Validation was conducted using 85 landslide occurrence points from 2025, obtained from the Wonogiri Regency Regional Disaster Management Agency (BPBD), with 12 of these points verified through field surveys. The results indicate that landslide susceptibility is categorized into four classes: low, moderate, high, and very high. The moderate susceptibility class covers the largest area. Validation results show that 57 occurrence points (67.06%) fall within the high susceptibility class, while 28 points (32.94%) fall within the moderate susceptibility class; no occurrence points were found in the low susceptibility class. These findings demonstrate that actual landslides occurred more frequently in areas classified as having high susceptibility compared to those with moderate susceptibility.

papers.summary: Intense rainfall events in the Mont Robinson region of New Caledonia frequently trigger shallow translational landslides on steep volcanic-sedimentary terrain. papers.title: Analisis Tingkat Kerawanan Longsor Lahan Di Kecamatan Ile Ape Timur Kabupaten Lembata Provinsi Nusa Tenggara Timur (NTT)
papers.source: UMS Library Center of Academic Activities (Universitas Muhammadiyah Surakarta)
papers.summary: Landslides are a common natural disaster in areas with steep topography, including Ile Ape Timur Subdistrict, Lembata Regency, East Nusa Tenggara. This disaster is caused by a combination of natural factors, such as high rainfall, slope gradients, soil types, and human activities that alter land use. This study aims to analyze the landslide susceptibility levels and identify mitigation efforts in Ile Ape Timur Subdistrict. This research employed a descriptive method with a Geographic Information System (GIS) approach. The data used included slope gradient maps, soil type maps, rainfall data, and land use maps, analyzed using a weighted overlay technique to produce a landslide susceptibility map. Primary data were collected through field observations, while secondary data were obtained from relevant agencies such as BPBD and PUPR of Lembata Regency. The results show that the landslide susceptibility levels in Ile Ape Timur are categorized into four classes: not susceptible (3,174 hectares), less susceptible (25 hectares), susceptible (718 hectares), and highly susceptible (6 hectares). The main factors influencing susceptibility are steep slopes, Andosols soil prone to erosion, and relatively high annual rainfall. Recommended mitigation efforts include structural approaches, such as terracing and the installation of early warning systems (EWS), as well as non-structural approaches, including community education and disaster simulations. This study is expected to serve as a basis for the government and local communities to implement effective landslide disaster mitigation measures, minimizing material losses and casualties.

papers.summary: Vegetation has been used for slope stabilization for centuries, with conventional measures like soil nails and piles serving to complement the root reinforcement. Vegetation contributes to reinforcement through mechanical reinforcement provided by the root, and hydro-mechanical effects associated with evapotranspiration. Despite decades of research, translating root reinforcement into engineering practice remains unclear because most studies focus on specific plant species rather than on mechanically meaningful root traits, limiting comparability and predictive capability. This paper provides a comprehensive review of root characteristics and root types relevant to mechanical root reinforcement, specifically root morphology (e.g., diameter) and architecture (e.g., orientation and root area ratio (RAR) distribution). It also reviews the state-of-the-art of existing methods for quantifying mechanical root reinforcement: theoretical models, experimental methods from laboratory to field-scale, and numerical approaches based on FEM and DEM. Building on identified gaps and the need for functional trait-based root classification, a three dimensional finite element model with an explicit representation of simplified roots is developed and validated against field scale direct shear tests on vegetated soil. Roads interrupt these controls by compressing peat and blocking lateral groundwater flow, producing persistent changes in water-table position, oxygen exposure, solute movement, and decomposition. papers.title: Effects of root architecture of different wheat cultivars on soil structure
papers.source: AMS Dottorato Institutional Doctoral Theses Repository (University of Bologna)
papers.summary: Plant roots play a crucial role in maintaining soil health by influencing physical structure and hydraulic properties. This study investigates relationships between root morphology of wheat genotypes and their impacts on soil structure and hydraulic characteristics. Using shovelomics, we characterized root systems of wheat cultivars (Paragon, Bologna) and landraces (Senatore-Cappelli, Watkins238) selected for contrasting root morphologies. X-ray computed tomography (CT) was applied to examine soil pore networks at cylinder and aggregate scales, while soil hydraulic properties were measured using Wind evaporation and dew point techniques. Results demonstrated significant genotype-driven differences in soil morphology and hydraulic functions. Structural analyses (Minkowski functionals, percolation theory) showed significant variability in bioporosity and pore connectivity among genotypes compared to bare soil. Senatore-Cappelli exhibited notably larger biopores (>1 mm diameter). Hydraulic characterization using a van Genuchten bimodal model revealed statistically significant differences in soil water retention curves and hydraulic conductivity among genotypes. Root traits, including total root length, branching frequency, lateral root length, and root diameter, significantly correlated with soil pore size distribution and hydraulic parameters. This analysis underscores the importance of root architecture in modulating soil structure and water dynamics, highlighting the potential of specific wheat genotypes to affect soil health, water retention, and agricultural sustainability.

papers.title: EFFECTS OF DOLOMITE AMENDMENTS ON PER- AND POLYFLUOROALKYL SUBSTANCES (PFAS) LEACHING IN AGRICULTURAL SOILS
papers.summary: Per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances (PFAS) are often found in agricultural soils due to land application of biosolids, wastewater-derived materials, and atmospheric deposition. However, PFAS transport behavior in variably saturated agricultural soils remains poorly studied. This study evaluates PFAS mobility within unsaturated soil using both intact soil cores (diameter: 3 inches, referred to as large columns (LC)) and packed, homogeneous soil columns (diameter: 1 inch, referred to as small columns (SC)) under the presence and absence of dolomite, which was recently reported to be able to reduce PFAS mobility through adsorption. All columns were amended with a biosolid (Milorganite) and half of the large and small columns received a powdered dolomite amendment at the surface. Columns were subjected to episodic infiltration based on precipitation data from 2019, and the leachate was collected at the base of each column for PFAS analysis. Our results showed that (1) the leaching of PFAS was strongly dependent on the structure and properties of the PFAS, and (2) dolomite amendments could lower the leaching of PFAS. The findings from this research will improve our quantitative understanding of how PFAS move through agricultural soils and the potential risks associated with land application, as well as the design and implementation of science-based management practices and regulation frameworks.

papers.summary: Water infiltration dynamics in block cave mining are critical to understanding and managing inrush hazards that threaten mine safety and operational continuity. This research investigates the development and flow behaviour of these pathways using an integrated physical and numerical modelling approach. papers.summary: Understanding subsurface water movement, particularly preferential water flow, is critical for water resource management and predicting contaminant transport. However, traditional invasive methods like dye staining experiments are destructive and only provide static information. Consequently, this thesis investigates the effectiveness of 3D time-lapse electrical resistivity tomography (ERT) for monitoring infiltration dynamics on a forested hillslope in Lower Austria. A Brilliant Blue saline tracer was applied to a 0.8 × 0.8 m plot during a two-hour irrigation event. papers.summary: Compacted clay barriers are central components of landfill liners and covers, clay cores in embankment dams and tailings facilities, and other geoenvironmental containment systems. Their design is traditionally governed by classification, plasticity, compaction, hydraulic conductivity, shear strength, compressibility, and construction-quality requirements. These criteria are essential, but they do not directly measure the resistance of a compacted clay barrier to the initiation and extension of open-mode discontinuities and the subsequent formation of connected preferential flow paths. papers.title: STUDI PERENCANAAN JALAN DAN PENGAMANAN LERENG PADA TRASE JALAN UJAN MAS PADA STA 0+050 SAMPAI STA 2+550
papers.summary: The development of safe and efficient road infrastructure is a crucial element in regional development. This study aims to conduct technical planning for new roads and slope protection systems on the Ujan Mas Road Trace (STA 0+050 to STA 2+550). Given the location's topography, which is dominated by steep slopes, this planning integrates geometric design of the road, pavement structure, drainage system, and retaining wall design. The study methodology includes primary and secondary data collection, hydrological analysis for the design flood discharge calculation, and soil mechanics investigation to ensure the stability of the retaining wall structure against overturning, shearing, and dynamic earthquake loads (Mononobe-Okabe method). In addition to technical aspects, this study also includes the preparation of a Cost Budget Plan (RAB) to accurately estimate construction funding requirements based on the calculated work volume. The geometric design of the road refers to the Bina Marga standard, while the pavement analysis uses the Bina Marga method. The final results of this study are expected to provide a comprehensive and economical technical solution for road infrastructure development in the area, while prioritizing safety aspects and sustainable slope stability

papers.title: Boundary Influence in Truncated Groundwater Models: Reconstructing a Local-Scale MODFLOW Model from a Consultant-Developed Regional Model in the Monterey Subbasin
papers.summary: Regional groundwater models built by consultants contain valuable calibrated frameworks but are often too large and complex for repeated local-scale analysis. Rather than rebuilding an entirely new smaller model, this study truncates the existing consultant-built regional model of the Monterey Subbasin, preserving the original grid structure and parameter framework while reducing the active domain to a manageable size for planning-level use. A key finding is that boundary-condition representation exerted a dominant influence on simulated groundwater behavior within the truncated domain, highlighting that truncation is a structural decision that meaningfully affects how the model responds. Model performance was evaluated two ways. Alternative hydraulic conductivity fields derived from AEM resistivity data were used to assess how sensitive the reconstructed model was to changes in internal parameter structure. Transient injection simulations produced cumulative groundwater mounding that grew progressively over repeated seasonal cycles, confirming realistic aquifer behavior and demonstrating the model's value as a practical and transparent planning-level tool.
